title: Of one defect in our government
paragraphs: My late father, a man whose only advantages were experience and his own natural gifts, but who had a very clear judgment, once told me he had had thoughts of trying to introduce this practice: that in every city there should be a fixed place where anyone in need of anything could go and have their business registered by an officer appointed for the purpose. For example: I need a buyer for my pearls; I need someone with pearls to sell; this one wants company on the road to Paris; that one is looking for a servant of such-and-such a kind; another for a master; another for some particular craftsman. Some looking for one thing, some for another, each according to his need. Without doubt, these mutual notices would be of no small benefit to public exchange and communication. There are always parties searching for one another, and for want of knowing each other's needs they are left in real distress.

I have heard — to the great shame of the age we live in — that two of the most learned men of our day died so poor they had hardly bread to put in their mouths: Lilius Gregorius Giraldus in Italy and Sebastianus Castalio in Germany. I am sure there are a thousand men who would have invited them into their families on advantageous terms, or relieved them where they were, had they only known of their want. The world is not so universally corrupted; I know a man who would gladly use the estate his ancestors left him, for as long as fortune allows him to enjoy it, to shelter rare and remarkable people of any kind whom misfortune sometimes persecutes to the last extreme, from the dangers of want — at least to place them in such a condition that they would have to be hard to please not to be content.

My father had this rule in his domestic affairs (which I know how to praise but by no means how to imitate): besides the day-book or household memorandum, where the small accounts, payments, and expenses that don't require a secretary's hand were entered, and which the steward kept, he had whoever wrote for him keep a journal, setting down in it all the noteworthy events and daily memorials of the history of the house. Very pleasant to look over when time begins to wear things out of memory, and very useful sometimes to settle a doubt about when this or that began, or ended; what visitors came, and when they left; our journeys, absences, marriages, deaths; news good or bad received; changes among the principal servants, and so on. An old custom, which I think it would do everyone good to revive in his own house. I see I was very foolish to neglect it.

title: Of the custom of wearing clothes
paragraphs: Whatever I say on this subject, I am bound to trespass on some of the boundaries of custom, so carefully has she sealed off every approach. I was debating with myself, this shivering season, whether the practice of going naked in those nations recently discovered is imposed on them by the heat of the climate — as we say of the Indians and Moors — or whether it is the original fashion of humankind. Men of understanding, since all things under the sun (as Scripture says) are subject to the same laws, used in such cases — where we have to separate the laws of nature from those invented by man — to look to the general order of the world, in which nothing can be counterfeit. Now, since all other creatures are sufficiently furnished with what they need to sustain themselves, it is hardly credible that we alone are brought into the world defective and needy, in a condition that cannot survive without outside help. So I believe that, just as plants, trees, and animals — everything that has life — are seen to be by nature sufficiently clothed and covered to protect them against the weather:
"Proptereaque fere res omnes aut corio sunt, Aut seta, aut conchis, aut callo, aut cortice tectae,"
["And for this reason almost all things are clothed with skin, or hair, or shells, or hide, or bark." — Lucretius, iv. 936.]

so were we; but, like people who put out the day's light by burning artificial light, we have, with borrowed forms and fashions, destroyed our own. And it is plain that custom alone makes impossible what is otherwise not so at all. For of those peoples who know nothing of clothing, some live in the same temperatures we do, and some in much colder climates. Besides, our most tender parts are always exposed to the air — the eyes, mouth, nose, ears — and our country labourers, like our ancestors in earlier times, go with their chests and bellies open. Had we been born with a built-in need for skirts and breeches, no doubt nature would have armoured the parts she meant to expose to the seasons with a thicker skin, as she has done at the fingertips and the soles of the feet. And why should this seem hard to believe? I notice much more distance between my own dress and that of one of our country labourers than between his and that of a man who has no other covering but his skin. How many men, especially in Turkey, go naked out of devotion? Someone asked a beggar, whom he saw walking around in his shirt in the depth of winter, as cheerful as a man wrapped up to the ears in furs, how he could stand to go like that. "Why, sir," he answered, "you go with your face bare; I am all face." The Italians tell a story of the Duke of Florence's fool. When the duke, warmly wrapped, asked him how he, so thinly clad, could bear the cold the duke himself could barely endure, the fool answered: "Try my recipe — put on all the clothes you own at once, and you'll feel no more cold than I do." King Massinissa, into extreme old age, could never be persuaded to cover his head, no matter how cold, stormy, or rainy the weather; the same is told of the Emperor Severus. Herodotus tells us that in the battles between Egyptians and Persians, both he and others observed that of the bodies left on the field the skulls of the Egyptians were beyond comparison harder than those of the Persians, because the latter had gone with their heads always covered from infancy — first with caps, then with turbans — while the others kept theirs always shaved and bare. King Agesilaus, into a decrepit old age, wore the same clothes in winter that he wore in summer. Caesar, says Suetonius, always marched at the head of his army, usually on foot, bareheaded whether it rained or shone; as much is said of Hannibal:
"Tum vertice nudo, Excipere insanos imbres, coelique ruinam."
["Bareheaded he marched through pelting rain and the sky's worst fury." — Silius Italicus, i. 250.]

A Venetian who has lived for a long time in Pegu, and who has lately come back from there, writes that the men and women of that kingdom, though they cover all their other parts, always go barefoot and even ride that way. And Plato strongly advises, for the health of the whole body, to give the head and feet no clothing other than what nature has provided. The man whom the Poles have elected as their king since ours came back from there — one of the greatest princes of the age — never wears gloves, and whatever the weather, in winter or otherwise, wears no other cap outdoors than he wears at home. I, on the other hand, can't stand to be unbuttoned or untied; my neighbouring labourers would feel themselves in chains if they were laced up like me. Varro thinks that when it was decreed we should be bareheaded in the presence of the gods and the magistrate, it was set up more for the sake of health, to harden us against the weather, than out of any sense of reverence. And since we are now on the subject of cold, and since the French used to wear all sorts of colours — not I, since I rarely wear anything but black or white, in imitation of my father — let us add another story from Captain Martin du Bellay, who reports that on the march to Luxembourg he saw such a great frost that the troops' ration-wine was cut with hatchets and wedges and given out to the soldiers by weight, who carried it away in baskets. And Ovid:
"Nudaque consistunt, formam servantia testae, Vina; nec hausta meri, sed data frusta, bibunt."
["And the wines stand bare, keeping the shape of the cask; they drink not gulps of wine, but lumps handed out to them." — Ovid, Trist., iii. 10, 23.]

At the mouth of Lake Maeotis the frosts are so sharp that on the very same ground where Mithridates' lieutenant had fought the enemy dry-shod and given them a serious defeat, the following summer he won a naval victory over them on the same place. The Romans fought at a real disadvantage in their engagement with the Carthaginians near Piacenza, because they went into battle with their blood congealed and their limbs numbed by the cold, while Hannibal had had great fires distributed through his camp to warm his soldiers, and oil given out so that, by rubbing themselves down, they could make their muscles more supple and active and fortify their pores against the violence of the air and freezing wind that raged that season.

The retreat the Greeks made from Babylon back to their own country is famous for the hardships and disasters they had to overcome. One of these: caught in the mountains of Armenia by a terrible snowstorm, they lost all sense of the country and of the roads, and once driven up there spent a day and a night without food or drink. Most of their cattle died, many of the men starved, several were struck blind by the force of the hail and the glare of the snow, many lost fingers and toes, and many were left stiff and motionless by the extreme cold — though still with their minds intact.
Alexander saw a nation where they bury their fruit trees in winter to protect them from being destroyed by the frost, and we ourselves can see the same.

As for clothing, the King of Mexico changed his outfit four times a day and never put the same one on again, using whatever he laid aside in continual gifts and rewards. And no pot, dish, or other utensil from his kitchen or table was ever served twice.

title: Of Cato the Younger
paragraphs: ["I am not possessed by this common error of judging others by what I am myself. I easily believe things in others that differ from me. Though I am bound to one form, I do not tie the world to it, as every man does. I believe and conceive a thousand ways of living contrary to the common one." — Florio, ed. 1613, p. 113.]

I am not guilty of the common error of judging another by myself. I easily believe in someone else a temperament opposite to my own; and though I find myself committed to one particular way, I do not bind others to it as so many do. I believe in and grasp a thousand contrary ways of life, and, unlike most people, I more readily accept difference than uniformity among us. I will, as openly as anyone could wish, release a man from my own moods and principles and consider him on his own terms. Though I am not continent myself, I sincerely approve the continence of the Feuillants and Capuchins and praise their way of life highly. I imagine myself into their place, and love and honour them all the more for being unlike me. I very much want each of us to be judged on his own, and not dragged into the implications of common examples. My own weakness does not at all diminish the esteem I owe to the strength and vigour of those who deserve it:
"Sunt qui nihil suadent, quam quod se imitari posse confidunt."
["There are those who recommend nothing except what they think they can themselves imitate." — Cicero, De Orator., c. 7.]

Crawling along on the slime of the earth, I do not for that reason stop watching, up in the clouds, the unreachable height of certain heroic souls. It is a lot for me to have my judgment sound and just, even if my actions cannot be; to keep this sovereign part, at least, free from corruption. It is something to have my will right and good even where my legs fail me. This age we live in, in our part of the world at least, has grown so dull that not just the practice but even the very imagination of virtue is faulty, and seems to be no more than college jargon:
"Virtutem verba putant, ut Lucum ligna:"
["They think virtue is mere words, as they think a sacred grove is mere wood." — Horace, Ep., i. 6, 31.]
"Quam vereri deberent, etiam si percipere non possent."
["Which they ought to reverence, even if they cannot comprehend it." — Cicero, Tusc. Quas., v. 2.]

It has become a trinket to hang in a cabinet or to dangle from the tongue, like an earring, for show only. There are no longer any virtuous actions to be found; those that have the look of virtue still have none of its essence, because profit, glory, fear, custom, and other such external causes are what put us up to producing them. Our justice too, our courage, our courtesy, can be called by those names — but only as they appear to others and present themselves to the public. In the doer they cannot be virtue, since there is another end in view, another moving cause. Now virtue acknowledges nothing as her own except what is done by herself and for herself alone.

In the great battle of Plataea, which the Greeks under Pausanias won against Mardonius and the Persians, the victors, when dividing the glory of the action according to their custom, gave the Spartan nation the highest credit for valour in the engagement. The Spartans, expert judges of virtue, came to decide which particular Spartan deserved the honour of having behaved best on that occasion. They found that Aristodemus had risked himself with greater bravery than any other; but they would not award him the prize, on the grounds that his courage had been driven by a wish to clear his name of the disgrace he had earned at Thermopylae and to die well so as to wipe out that earlier stain.

Our judgments are still sick, and obey the temper of our corrupt manners. I notice that most of the wits of these times claim cleverness by trying to tarnish and darken the glory of the bravest and most generous deeds of former ages, putting some mean interpretation on them and inventing trivial causes and motives for the noble things they did. A great subtlety, indeed! Give me the greatest and least blemished action the world has ever seen and I will dream up a hundred plausible aims and ends to discredit it. God knows, if you draw them out fully, what range of motives our inner wills are open to. They don't so much play the censor maliciously as practise their detractions ignorantly and crudely.

The same effort and licence others spend on smudging and slandering these illustrious names, I would gladly take up to lend them my shoulder and raise them higher. These rare figures, picked out by the consensus of the wisest men of all ages as examples for the world, I would not hesitate to magnify in honour, as far as my invention would allow, by every favourable interpretation; and we may well believe that the force of our imagination falls infinitely short of their merit. It is the duty of good men to picture virtue as beautifully as they can; and there would be nothing wrong if our passion carried us a little away in favour of so sacred a form. What these other people do, on the contrary, they do either out of malice or from the vice of limiting their belief to their own capacity — or, what I am more inclined to think, because their eyes are not strong, clear, and lifted enough to take in the splendour of virtue in her native purity. Plutarch complains that in his own time some put the cause of the younger Cato's death down to fear of Caesar, at which he is rightly indignant; from which one can gather how much more offended he would have been with those who attributed it to ambition. Senseless people! Cato would rather have done a noble, just, and generous deed and been rewarded with disgrace than with glory. That man was, in truth, a pattern nature chose to show how high human virtue and constancy could reach.

But I am not equal to handling so rich a subject, and so I will only line up five Latin poets in competition praising Cato — and, incidentally, themselves. Now, a well-educated child will find the first two, compared with the others, a little flat and faint; the third more vigorous, but overdone by the extravagance of his own force. He will then judge there is room for one or two more steps of invention to reach the fourth, and on reaching that he will raise his hands in admiration. Coming to the last, separated by some distance from the first (a distance he will swear no human wit can fill), he will be astonished, he will not know where he is.

And here is the wonder: we have far more poets than judges or interpreters of poetry. It is easier to write it than to understand it. There is, indeed, a certain low and middling sort of poetry that can be judged by set rules of art; but true, supreme, divine poetry is above all rules and reason. Whoever discerns its beauty with the surest and steadiest sight sees no more than the quick flash of a lightning bolt: it does not exercise the judgment but ravishes and overwhelms it. The fury that possesses the man capable of penetrating it wounds a third person too, by hearing him recite it — like a magnet that not only draws the needle but also gives the needle the power to draw others. And it is even more clearly visible in our theatres: the sacred inspiration of the Muses first stirs the poet to anger, sorrow, hatred, or whatever they please, beyond himself; through the poet it then possesses the actor, and through the actor in turn, all the spectators. That is how our passions hang upon and depend on one another.

Poetry has had this power over me from childhood, to pierce me through and carry me away; but this vivid feeling, natural to me, has been handled differently by different forms — not so much higher or lower (since they were always the highest of their kind) as different in colour. First, a gay and sprightly fluency; then a lofty and penetrating subtlety; and finally a mature and steady vigour. Their names will say it better: Ovid, Lucan, Virgil.
But our poets are beginning their race:
"Sit Cato, dum vivit, sane vel Caesare major,"
["Let Cato, while he lives, be considered greater than Caesar himself." — Martial, vi. 32]
says one.
"Et invictum, devicta morte, Catonem,"
["And Cato unconquered, conquering death itself." — Manilius, Astron., iv. 87.]
says the second. And the third, speaking of the civil wars between Caesar and Pompey:
"Victrix causa diis placuit, sed victa Catoni."
["The victorious cause pleased the gods, the defeated one pleased Cato." — Lucan, i. 128.]
And the fourth, on the praises of Caesar:
"Et cuncta terrarum subacta, Praeter atrocem animum Catonis."
["And all the earth subdued, except the unyielding mind of Cato." — Horace, Od., ii. 1, 23.]
And the master of the choir, after parading all the great names of the greatest Romans, ends with this:
"His dantem jura Catonem."
["Cato giving laws to all the rest." — Aeneid, viii. 670.]

title: That we laugh and cry for the same thing
paragraphs: When we read in the histories that Antigonus was deeply displeased with his son for presenting him with the head of King Pyrrhus his enemy, freshly killed fighting against him, and that he wept on seeing it; that René, Duke of Lorraine, also mourned the death of Charles, Duke of Burgundy, whom he had himself defeated, and appeared in mourning at his funeral; and that at the battle of D'Auray (which Count Montfort won over Charles de Blois, his rival for the duchy of Brittany) the victor, meeting his enemy's dead body, was deeply afflicted at his death — we should not be too quick to cry:
"E cosi avven, che l'animo ciascuna Sua passion sotto 'l contrario manto, Ricopre, con la vista or'chiara, or'bruna."
["And so it happens that the soul veils each of its passions under the opposite cloak — its look now bright, now overcast." — Petrarch.]

When Pompey's head was presented to Caesar, the histories tell us, he turned his face away from it as from a sad and disagreeable sight. There had been such a long understanding and partnership between them in handling public affairs, such a community of fortunes, so many mutual services, so close an alliance, that this expression of his should not be misread, nor suspected as false or counterfeit, as this other writer would have it:
"Tutumque putavit Jam bonus esse socer; lacrymae non sponte cadentes, Effudit, gemitusque expressit pectore laeto;"
["And now he thought it safe to play the kind father-in-law — shedding forced tears and squeezing groans from a joyful breast." — Lucan, ix. 1037.]
For though it is true that most of our actions are nothing but mask and disguise, and it may sometimes be the case that
"Haeredis fletus sub persona risus est,"
["The heir's tears behind the mask are laughter." — Publius Syrus, apud Gellium, xvii. 14.]

still, in judging such episodes, we have to take into account how often our souls are stirred by several passions at once. Just as in our bodies there is, they say, a mixture of different humours, of which one is dominant according to our complexion and usually predominates in us, so the soul, though it has many motions agitating it, must necessarily have one to overrule the rest — though not with so necessary and absolute a dominion that, given the soul's pliancy and inconstancy, the less authoritative ones cannot reclaim their place on occasion and stage a little sally of their own. That is why we see not only children, who innocently follow nature, laugh and cry at the same thing, but also why none of us, on a journey we have set our heart on, can say that at the moment of parting with family and friends he doesn't feel something tugging at him inside; and even if he holds back his tears, he puts his foot in the stirrup with a sad and clouded face. And whatever gentle flame warms the heart of a modest and well-born young woman, she still has to be pried from her mother's neck and put to bed with her husband — whatever this jolly companion may say:
"Estne novis nuptis odio Venus? anne parentum Frustrantur falsis gaudia lachrymulis, Ubertim thalami quasi intra limina fundunt? Non, ita me divi, vera gemunt, juverint."

["Is Venus really so hateful to new brides, or do they cheat their parents' joy with false tears, weeping copiously almost at the very threshold of the bridal chamber? No — so help me the gods — they do not truly grieve." — Catullus, lxvi. 15.]

["Is Venus really so repugnant to newly married girls? Do they answer their parents' smiles with feigned tears? They weep copiously at the very threshold of the nuptial chamber. No — so the gods help me — they do not truly grieve." — Catullus, lxvi. 15.]

Nor is it strange to mourn someone dead whom you would by no means want alive again. When I scold my servant, I do it with all the spirit I have and load him with curses that are not pretended but downright real; yet, once the heat is over, if he should need me, I am perfectly ready to do him good — I instantly turn the page. When I call him calf and blockhead, I don't pretend to fasten those titles on him for ever; nor do I think I'm contradicting myself when, right after, I call him an honest fellow. No single quality holds us pure and entire. If it weren't a fool's habit to talk to oneself, scarcely a day or hour would go by without someone hearing me grumble and mutter to myself and against myself, "Damn fool!" — and yet I don't take that for my definition. Whoever sees me one moment cold and a moment later very affectionate toward my wife, and concludes that one or the other is faked, is an ass. Nero, taking leave of his mother whom he was sending to be drowned, was still moved at the farewell, struck with horror and pity. They say the light of the sun is not one continuous thing, but that he sends out fresh rays so densely upon one another that we cannot perceive the gaps:
"Largus enim liquidi fons luminis, aetherius sol, Irrigat assidue coelum candore recenti, Suppeditatque novo confestim lumine lumen."
["For the broad fount of liquid light, the heavenly sun, ceaselessly waters the sky with fresh brilliance, and at once supplies new light upon light." — Lucretius, v. 282.]
Just so, the soul darts out her passions variously and imperceptibly.

Artabanus, coming suddenly upon his nephew Xerxes, scolded him for the sudden change in his face. Xerxes was looking out at the immense size of his forces crossing the Hellespont for the Grecian expedition: first he was seized with a thrill of joy at seeing so many millions of men under his command, and this showed in the gaiety of his expression; but then it struck him that of all those lives, within a century at most, not one would be left — and at once his brow darkened and he grew sad, even to tears.

We have stubbornly pursued the revenge for an injury and felt a singular satisfaction at the victory; but we will still weep. We are not weeping for the victory; nothing has changed in that. But the soul looks at things with another eye and represents them to itself with another sort of face — for everything has many faces and many aspects.
Relatives, old friends, long acquaintance take hold of our imaginations and, for the time, soften them according to their condition; but the turn is so quick that it is gone in a moment:
"Nil adeo fieri celeri ratione videtur, Quam si mens fieri proponit, et inchoat ipsa, Ocius ergo animus, quam res se perciet ulla, Ante oculos quorum in promptu natura videtur;"
["Nothing seems to happen so quickly as what the mind proposes and itself begins. The mind moves faster than anything we see in nature." — Lucretius, iii. 183.]

and so, if we tried to make one continuous thing out of all this succession of passions, we would be deceiving ourselves. When Timoleon laments the murder he carried out after such mature and noble deliberation, he is not lamenting the freedom restored to his country, nor the tyrant; he is lamenting his brother. One part of his duty is done; let us allow him to do the other.

title: Of solitude
paragraphs: Let us set aside that long comparison between the active and the solitary life; and as for the fine sayings with which ambition and greed disguise their vices — that we are not born for ourselves but for the public — let us boldly turn to those who are actually in public affairs. Let them lay their hands on their hearts and then say whether, on the contrary, they don't seek titles and offices and the world's tumult precisely to make their private advantage at public expense. The corrupt routes by which, in our time, they reach the height their ambition aims at make it clear enough that their ends cannot be very good. Let us tell ambition that she herself is what gives us a taste for solitude — for what does she avoid so much as company? What does she seek so much as elbow room? A man can live well or badly anywhere; but if what Bias says is true, that the greater part is the worse part, or what Ecclesiastes says, that there is not one good man in a thousand:
"Rari quippe boni: numero vix sunt totidem quot Thebarum portae, vel divitis ostia Nili,"
["Good men are rare: there are barely as many as the gates of Thebes or the mouths of the rich Nile." — Juvenal, Sat., xiii. 26.]

the contagion is very dangerous in a crowd. A man must either imitate the vicious or hate them — both dangerous, either to resemble them because they are many or to hate many because they are different from us. Merchants who go to sea are right to be careful that those they sail with are not dissolute blasphemers or otherwise vicious; they regard such company as unlucky. That is why Bias said, with a smile, to those who, caught in a dangerous storm with him, were calling on the gods: "Hush, speak softly, so they may not know you are here in my company." And, more telling still, Albuquerque, viceroy in the Indies for King Emmanuel of Portugal, in an extreme peril of shipwreck, took a young boy upon his shoulders for this sole reason: that in the shared danger the boy's innocence might serve to recommend him to the divine favour and bring them safe to shore. It isn't that a wise man cannot live contented anywhere and be alone even in the middle of a palace crowd; but if it is left to his choice, the schoolman will tell you he should flee the very sight of the crowd. He will put up with it if he must; but if it is up to him, he will choose to be alone. He cannot think himself sufficiently free of vice if he still has to contend with it in other men. Charondas punished as evildoers those convicted of keeping bad company. There is nothing so unsociable and so sociable as man — the one through his vice, the other through his nature. And Antisthenes, in my view, did not give a good enough answer when someone reproached him for frequenting bad company by saying that doctors live well enough among the sick — for if doctors contribute to the patients' health, they cannot help, through contagion, constant exposure to disease, and familiarity with it, impairing their own.

Now the aim, I take it, is one and the same: to live more at leisure, more at our ease. But people do not always go the right way about it. They often think they have given up business entirely when they have only swapped one occupation for another. Running a private household is hardly less trouble than running a kingdom. Wherever the mind is troubled, it is wholly disordered, and domestic concerns are no less wearing for being less important. Besides, having shaken off the court and the marketplace, we have not shaken off the principal vexations of life:
"Ratio et prudentia curas, Non locus effusi late maris arbiter, aufert;"
["Reason and prudence, not a place commanding a view of the wide sea, take cares away." — Horace, Ep., i. 2.]
ambition, greed, indecision, fear, and unruly desires do not leave us just because we leave our native country:
"Et Post equitem sedet atra cura;"
["And black care sits behind the rider." — Horace, Od., iii. 1, 40].
they often follow us right into cloisters and philosophical schools; no desert, no cave, no hair shirt, no fast can shake us free of them:
"Haeret lateri lethalis arundo."
["The fatal shaft sticks fast in her side." — Aeneid, iv. 73.]
Someone telling Socrates that a certain person was no better for all his travels: "I quite believe it," said Socrates, "for he took himself along."
"Quid terras alio calentes Sole mutamus? patriae quis exsul Se quoque fugit?"
["Why do we trade our land for one warmed by another sun? Who, in exile from his country, has also fled from himself?" — Horace, Od., ii. 16, 18.]

If a man does not first unload himself, and his mind, of the burden he finds himself carrying, motion will only make it press harder and sit heavier — just as a ship's cargo is less troublesome when it is fixed and settled in place. You do more harm than good to a sick man by moving him from place to place; you fix and entrench his disease by motion, as stakes are driven deeper and more firmly into the earth by being worked up and down in the spot where they're meant to stand. So it isn't enough to remove yourself from the public; it isn't enough to change the soil — a man must flee the popular habits that have taken root in his soul, must withdraw and come home to himself:
"Rupi jam vincula, dicas Nam luctata canis nodum arripit; attamen illi, Quum fugit, a collo trahitur pars longa catenae."
["You may say, 'I have broken my chains' — but a dog, after a long struggle, may snap the knot and still drag a long piece of the chain from its collar as it runs." — Persius, Sat., v. 158.]
We still carry our fetters along with us. It is no real freedom — we still glance back at what we have left behind us; the imagination is still full of it:

"Nisi purgatum est pectus, quae praelia nobis Atque pericula tunc ingratis insinuandum? Quantae conscindunt hominem cupedinis acres Sollicitum curae? quantique perinde timores? Quidve superbia, spurcitia, ac petulantia, quantas Efficiunt clades? quid luxus desidiesque?"

["But unless the mind is purified, what inner battles and dangers we then incur in spite of ourselves! How many bitter anxieties, how many fears follow on unbridled passion! What ruin pride, lust, and petulant anger work on us! What evils luxury and sloth bring!" — Lucretius, v. 4.]
Our disease lies in the mind, which cannot escape from itself;
"In culpa est animus, qui se non effugit unquam," — Horace, Ep., i. 14, 13.
and so it must be called home and confined to itself: that is the true solitude, and it can be enjoyed even in populous cities and in the courts of kings — though more comfortably apart.

Now, since we intend to live alone and to do without all manner of social commerce, let us arrange things so that our contentment depends wholly on ourselves. Let us dissolve all the bonds that tie us to others; let us secure from ourselves the ability to live alone in good earnest, and to live at our ease too.

When Stilpo had escaped the burning of his town, where he lost his wife, his children, and his goods, Demetrius Poliorcetes, seeing him appear undisturbed amid such a ruin of his country, asked him whether he had suffered no loss. Stilpo answered, No; and that, thank God, nothing of his had been lost. This was also what the philosopher Antisthenes meant when he said wryly that "a man should furnish himself with such things as would float, and that could escape the storm with their owner." And indeed a wise man never loses anything if he has himself. When the city of Nola was destroyed by the barbarians, Paulinus, who was bishop of the place, having lost everything he had and being himself a prisoner, prayed like this: "O Lord, keep me from feeling this loss; for you know that they have not yet touched anything of what is truly mine." The riches that made him rich and the goods that made him good were still intact. This is what it is to choose treasures that can defend themselves from plunder and violence, and to hide them in a place no one can enter and that can only be betrayed by ourselves. Wives, children, goods are to be had, and especially health, by those who can get them; but we are not to set our hearts on them so far that our happiness depends on them. We must reserve a back-shop, wholly our own and entirely free, in which to set up our true liberty, our chief solitude and retreat. There we are mostly to keep our own company, and so privately that no foreign acquaintance or commerce is admitted; there to laugh and to talk as if without wife, children, goods, retinue, or attendance — so that when it falls out that we must lose any or all of them, it will be no new thing for us to be without them. We have a mind pliable enough in itself to be company; it has what is needed to attack and defend, to receive and to give. Let us not, then, fear that we shall languish in this solitude under a dreary emptiness.
"In solis sis tibi turba locis."
["In solitude, be a crowd to yourself." — Tibullus, vi. 13. 12.]

Virtue is satisfied with herself, without discipline, without speeches, without effects. Of our ordinary actions there is not one in a thousand that really concerns us. The man you see scrambling up the ruins of that wall, in a fury and transported, with so many musket shots aimed at him; and the other, scarred all over, pale and faint with hunger, yet resolved to die rather than open the gates to him — do you think they are there for their own sake? No: they are there perhaps for someone they never saw, who never gives a thought to their pains and danger but lounges meanwhile in sloth and pleasure. And that drooling, bleary-eyed, slovenly fellow you see coming out of his study after midnight — do you think he has been poring over books to learn how to be a better, wiser, more contented man? Nothing of the sort. He will end his days at it, but he will teach posterity the metre of Plautus' verses and the right spelling of a Latin word. Who is it that does not willingly trade his health, his rest, and his very life for reputation and glory — the most useless, frivolous, false coin that circulates among us? Our own death does not trouble and terrify us enough; let us, on top of it, take on those of our wives, our children, our family. Our own affairs don't give us anxiety enough; let us take on those of our neighbours and friends, the better to wreck and torment ourselves:
"Vah! quemquamne hominem in animum instituere, aut Parare, quod sit carius, quam ipse est sibi?"
["Ah! can any man set up in his mind, or fix on, something dearer to him than he is to himself?" — Terence, Adelph., i. I, 13.]

Solitude seems to me to wear its best face for those who have already spent their most active and flourishing years in the world's service, after the example of Thales. We have lived enough for others; let us at least live out the small remnant of life for ourselves. Let us now draw in our thoughts and intentions to ourselves, to our own ease and rest. It is no light thing to make a safe retreat; it will be enough for us to do this without mixing in other enterprises. Since God gives us leave to arrange our departure, let us pack our bags, take leave in good time of the company, and untangle ourselves from those violent demands that pull us elsewhere and separate us from ourselves.

We must break the knot of our obligations, however strong; from now on we may love this thing or that, but marry nothing except ourselves. That is to say: let everything else be our own, but not so attached and so close that it cannot be torn off without flaying us or tearing out part of our whole. The greatest thing in the world is for a man to know that he is his own. It is time to wean ourselves from society when we can no longer add anything to it; whoever is not in a condition to lend must forbid himself to borrow. Our forces are beginning to fail; let us call them in and concentrate them in and for ourselves. Let whoever can cast off within himself, and dissolve, the offices of friendship and company, do so. In this decline of nature that makes him useless, burdensome, and a nuisance to others, let him take care not to be useless, burdensome, and a nuisance to himself. Let him soothe and care for himself, and above all govern himself with such reverence for his reason and conscience that he is ashamed to take a false step in their presence:
"Rarum est enim, ut satis se quisque vereatur."
["For it is rare that men feel enough respect and reverence for themselves." — Quintilian, x. 7.]

Socrates says that boys should have themselves instructed, grown men should exercise themselves in doing well, and old men should withdraw from all civil and military employments, living as they choose, without obligation to any office. Some temperaments are more suited to these counsels of retirement than others. People of soft and slow apprehension, of a tender will and affection, not easily put to work — among whom I count myself, both by nature and by reflection — will take to this advice more readily than active, busy souls, who embrace everything, throw themselves into everything, are hot for everything, offering and giving themselves up to every occasion. We are to make use of these accidental, external commodities so far as they please us, but by no means to lay our principal foundation on them; that is not a real one; neither nature nor reason allows it. Why, then, should we, against their laws, enslave our own contentment to another's power? To anticipate as well the accidents of fortune — to deprive ourselves of the conveniences we have in our own power, as some have done out of devotion and certain philosophers by reasoning; to be one's own servant, to lie hard, to put out one's own eyes, to throw one's wealth into the river, to go in search of grief; some aiming through this life's misery at bliss in another, others by laying themselves low to avoid the danger of falling — all such things are acts of an excessive virtue. The toughest and most resolute natures make even their seclusion glorious and exemplary:

"Tuta et parvula laudo, Quum res deficiunt, satis inter vilia fortis Verum, ubi quid melius contingit et unctius, idem Hos sapere et solos aio bene vivere, quorum Conspicitur nitidis fundata pecunia villis."

["When means run short, I praise a safe and modest condition, content with little; but when things grow better and richer, I say all the same that only those are wise and live well whose invested money shows in handsome villas." — Horace, Ep., i. 15, 42.]

A good deal less would do for me. It is enough for me, under fortune's favour, to prepare myself for her disgrace, and, while I am at ease, to picture to myself, as far as imagination can stretch, the trouble to come — as we do in jousts and tournaments, where we play at war in the deepest calm of peace. I do not think Arcesilaus the philosopher any less temperate and virtuous for the fact that he was known to use gold and silver vessels when his fortune allowed; indeed I think better of him than if he had denied himself what he used with liberality and moderation. I can see the utmost limits of natural necessity; and when I see a poor man begging at my door, often more cheerful and healthier than I am, I put myself in his place and try to fit my mind to his manner. Running through other examples in the same way, even when I picture death, poverty, contempt, and sickness at my heels, I easily resolve not to be alarmed, since someone less than I bears them so patiently; and I won't believe that a smaller understanding can do more than a greater, or that the effects of precept cannot rise as high as those of habit. And knowing how uncertain the duration of these accidental conveniences is, I never forget, in the height of all my enjoyments, to make it my chief prayer to Almighty God that He will be pleased to make me content with myself and with the condition I am in. I see young men, very gay and lively, who nevertheless keep a stock of pills in their trunk at home, ready when a cold comes — which they fear the less because they think they have a remedy on hand. Everyone should do the same; and if, moreover, they find themselves prone to some more violent disease, they should provide themselves with medicines that can numb and deaden the affected part.

The occupation a man chooses for such a life should be neither laborious nor unpleasant; otherwise there is no point in retiring at all. And that depends on each person's taste and temperament. Mine has no kind of liking for husbandry, and those who do love it ought to apply themselves to it in moderation:
["I try to make circumstances submit to me, not myself to circumstances." — Horace, Ep., i. i, 19.]

Husbandry is otherwise a very servile employment, as Sallust calls it; though some parts of it are more excusable than the rest — like the care of gardens, which Xenophon credits to Cyrus. A middle ground can be found between the sordid, low application, full of perpetual anxiety, that you see in men who make it their whole business and study, and the dull, extreme negligence that lets everything go to ruin, as you see in others:
"Democriti pecus edit agellos Cultaque, dum peregre est animus sine corpore velox."
["Democritus' cattle eat his corn and trample his fields, while his soaring mind ranges abroad without the body." — Horace, Ep., i, 12, 12.]

But let us hear what advice the younger Pliny gives his friend Caninius Rufus on the subject of solitude: "I advise you, in the full and plentiful retirement you have, to leave the care of husbandry to your labourers, and to give yourself up to the study of letters, and to draw from it something that may be entirely and absolutely your own." By which he means reputation — like Cicero, who says he would use his solitude and retirement from public affairs to acquire by his writings an immortal life:
"Usque adeone Scire tuum, nihil est, nisi te scire hoc, sciat alter?"
["Is your knowledge worth nothing at all, unless someone else knows that you know it?" — Persius, Sat., i. 23.]

It seems only reasonable, when a man talks of retiring from the world, that he should look entirely out of it. These men do it only by halves: they plan well enough for themselves for the time when they will no longer be in it, but they still mean to gather the fruits of that plan from the world after they have left it — which is a ridiculous contradiction.

The imagination of those who seek solitude out of devotion, filling their hopes and their courage with the certainty of divine promises in the other life, is far more rationally grounded. They set before themselves God, an object infinite in goodness and power; there the soul has, at full liberty, the means to satisfy her desires; afflictions and sufferings turn to their advantage, since they are borne for the acquisition of eternal health and joy; death is to be wished for and longed for as the passage to so perfect a condition; the severity of the rules they impose on themselves is soon softened by habit, and all their carnal appetites baffled and subdued by being refused indulgence and food — for these appetites are sustained only by use and exercise. This single goal of another, happily immortal life is what really deserves that we should give up the pleasures and conveniences of this one; and whoever can really and steadily kindle his soul with the heat of this living faith and hope builds for himself in solitude a more delightful and luxurious life than any other.

Neither the end, then, nor the means of Pliny's advice please me, for we often jump out of the frying-pan into the fire. This book-occupation is as wearing as any other, and as great an enemy to health, which ought to be the first consideration; nor should a man let himself be lured by the pleasure of it, which is the same kind of pleasure that ruins the frugal, the greedy, the voluptuous, and the ambitious.

["This plodding occupation of books is as painful as any other, and as great an enemy to health, which ought principally to be considered. And a man should not let himself be inveigled by the pleasure he takes in them." — Florio, edit. 1613, p. 122.]

The sages warn us often enough to beware the treachery of our desires, and to distinguish true and entire pleasures from those that are mixed up and complicated with greater pain. For most of our pleasures, they say, coax and caress us only to strangle us, like those thieves the Egyptians called Philistae. If the headache came before the drunkenness, we would be careful about drinking too much; but pleasure, to fool us, marches in front and hides her train. Books are pleasant; but if, by over-studying, we damage our health and ruin our good humour — the best parts we have — then let us give it up. I, for my part, am one of those who think no fruit drawn from books can make up for so great a loss. As men who have long felt themselves weakened by illness finally give themselves up to the mercy of medicine and submit to certain rules of living they are never afterwards to break, so the man who retires, tired and disgusted with the common way of life, should model this new life he is entering by the rules of reason, and set it up and establish it by deliberate thought and reflection. He should take leave of all kinds of labour, whatever advantage they may promise, and in general shake off the passions that disturb the peace of body and soul, and then choose the way that best suits his own temper:
"Unusquisque sua noverit ire via."

In husbandry, in study, in hunting, and in every other pursuit, we are to go to the utmost limits of pleasure, but to take care against going further, where trouble begins to mix in with it. We are to keep only as much activity as is needed to keep us in breath and to defend us from the inconveniences of the other extreme — dull, stupid laziness. There are sterile, knotty branches of knowledge, hammered out chiefly for the crowd; let them be left to those who are engaged in the world's service. For myself, I care for no books except either those that are pleasant and easy, to amuse me, or those that comfort me and instruct me how to regulate my life and my death:
"Tacitum sylvas inter reptare salubres, Curantem, quidquid dignum sapienti bonoque est."
["Silently wandering among the healthy groves, attending to whatever is worthy of a wise and good man." — Horace, Ep., i. 4, 4.]

Wiser men, with great strength and vigour of soul, may set themselves a wholly spiritual rest; but for me, who have a very ordinary soul, it is absolutely necessary to support myself with bodily comforts. And since age has of late deprived me of the pleasures that were more agreeable to me, I instruct and sharpen my appetite for those that remain, which suit this new stage. We should hold on with all our force, both hands and teeth, to the use of the pleasures of life that the years, one after another, snatch from us:
"Carpamus dulcia; nostrum est, Quod vivis; cinis, et manes, et fabula fies."
["Let us gather life's sweets — what you have while you live is yours. Soon you will be ashes, a ghost, a story." — Persius, Sat., v. 151.]

Now, as to the end that Pliny and Cicero set before us — glory — it is infinitely far from my account. Ambition is, of all dispositions, the most contrary to solitude; glory and rest are things that simply cannot live in the same place. As far as I can see, these men have only their arms and legs out of the crowd; their soul and intention remain confined behind it more than ever:
"Tun', vetule, auriculis alienis colligis escas?"
["Do you, then, old man, gather food for others' ears?" — Persius, Sat., i. 22.]

they have only stepped back to take a better leap, and with a stronger motion to plunge into the crowd again. Do you want to see how short they fall? Let us set against them the advice of two philosophers from two very different sects, writing — the one to Idomeneus, the other to Lucilius, their friends — urging them to retire into solitude from worldly honours and affairs. "You have," they say, "so far lived swimming and floating; come now and die in port. You have given the first part of your life to the light; give what remains to the shade. It is impossible to give up business unless you also give up its fruit; so disengage yourselves from all concern for fame and glory. The brilliance of your past actions risks following you into your most private retreat and giving you too much light. Give up, along with the other pleasures, the one that comes from another man's approval; and as for your knowledge and gifts, don't worry about them — they will not lose their effect provided you yourselves are the better for them. Remember the man who, asked why he took such pains in an art that could be appreciated by only a few, replied: 'A few are enough for me; one is enough; none would still be enough.' He spoke truly: you and a companion are theatre enough for one another, or you are enough for yourself. Let the people be one to you, and be one to the whole people. It is an unworthy ambition to want to draw glory from one's idleness and privacy. You should do as the hunted beasts do, who efface their tracks at the entrance to their den. You are no longer to concern yourself with how the world talks of you, but how you are to talk to yourself. Retire into yourself — but first prepare yourself there to receive yourself. It would be folly to trust yourself in your own hands if you can't govern yourself. A man can come to grief alone as well as in company. Until you have made yourself into someone before whom you would not dare to slip, until you have a sense of shame and respect for yourself,
"Obversentur species honestae animo;"
["Let honest images be ever present to the mind." — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., ii. 22.]

keep continually before your imagination Cato, Phocion, and Aristides, in whose presence even fools would hide their faults; make them the controllers of all your intentions. Should those intentions stray from virtue, your respect for these men will put you right; they will keep you on the path of being contented with yourself, of borrowing nothing from anyone but yourself, of holding and fixing your soul on certain and limited thoughts in which she can take pleasure, and, having understood the true and real goods — which men enjoy the more, the more they understand them — of resting satisfied, without any desire to prolong life or name." This is the precept of the true and natural philosophy, not of a boastful, chattering philosophy like the other two.

title: A consideration upon Cicero
paragraphs: One more word by way of comparison between these two. There are to be gathered, out of the writings of Cicero and the younger Pliny (who, in my opinion, resembled his uncle in his temperament very little), endless evidences of an immeasurably ambitious nature; and among others, this one: that both of them publicly solicit the historians of their time not to leave them out of their memoirs. And fortune, as if in spite, has kept the vanity of those requests on record down to our own day, while she long ago consigned the histories themselves to oblivion. But this surpasses any meanness of spirit in men of their standing — to think to draw great renown from chatter and verbal display, even publishing their private letters to their friends, and so doing it that, though some of them were never sent (the chance having gone), they still brought them to light with this fine excuse: that they were unwilling to waste their labours and lucubrations. Was it really becoming for two consuls of Rome, sovereign magistrates of the republic that ruled the world, to spend their leisure crafting clever, elegant letters in order to get a reputation for being good at their own mother tongue? Even a wretched schoolmaster, whose trade was teaching for a living, could hardly have done worse. If the deeds of Xenophon and Caesar had not far surpassed their eloquence, I scarcely believe they would have taken the pains to record them; they made it their business to recommend not their speaking but their doing. And if the perfection of eloquence could have added a lustre worthy of a great man, certainly Scipio and Laelius would never have surrendered the honour of their comedies, with all the luxuriance and elegance of the Latin tongue, to an African slave; for the work was theirs — its beauty and excellence say so clearly enough; Terence himself confesses as much; and I would take it ill from anyone who tried to dispossess me of that belief.

It is a kind of mockery and offence to praise a man for qualities unsuited to his station, even when they are otherwise commendable in themselves — qualities that should not, in any case, be his chief talent. As if one were to praise a king for being a good painter, a good architect, a fine shot, or a good runner at the ring: praises that bring no honour unless mentioned alongside, and in the train of, the qualities properly applicable to him, namely justice and the science of governing and conducting his people both in peace and in war. By the same token, agriculture was an honour to Cyrus, and eloquence and learning to Charlemagne. I have known some in my time who acquired both their titles and their fortunes by writing, and who then disowned their apprenticeship, corrupted their style, and affected ignorance of so vulgar a quality (which, in our nation, is held to be rarely found in very learned hands), and sought a reputation through better qualities. Demosthenes' companions on the embassy to Philip, praising that prince as handsome, eloquent, and a strong drinker, were told by Demosthenes that those were compliments more suited to a woman, a lawyer, or a sponge than to a king:
"Imperet bellante prior, jacentem Lenis in hostem."
["Let him overcome the enemy in battle, and be merciful to him when he is down." — Horace, Carm. Saec., v. 51.]
It isn't his job to know how to hunt or to dance well;
"Orabunt causas alii, coelique meatus Describent radio, et fulgentia sidera dicent; Hic regere imperio populos sciat."
["Let others plead cases at the bar, describe the courses of the heavens with a pointer, and name the gleaming stars; let this man know how to rule the nations." — Aeneid, vi. 849.]

Plutarch goes further: to show himself excellent in these less necessary qualities is to bear witness against a man himself — that he has spent his time and applied his study badly, when both should have been used to acquire more necessary and more useful things. So Philip, king of Macedon, having heard his son, the great Alexander, sing once at a feast to the amazement of the best musicians present, said to him: "Aren't you ashamed to sing so well?" And to that same Philip a musician, with whom he was arguing about some matters of his art, said: "Heaven forbid, sir, that so great a misfortune should ever fall on you as to understand these things better than I do." A king should be able to answer as Iphicrates did the orator who pressed him in invective: "And what are you, that you crow at this rate? Are you a man-at-arms, an archer, a pikeman?" — "I am none of these; but I know how to command them all." And Antisthenes took it as a sign of little worth in Ismenias that he was praised for playing the flute excellently well.

I know perfectly well that when I hear someone dwelling on the language of my essays, I would rather he said nothing at all: that is not so much elevating the style as belittling the matter, all the more offensively for being done obliquely. And yet I am much mistaken if many other writers offer more substance worth noting on the subject; well or badly written, no one else, I think, has set down on paper more solid things, or, at any rate, more straightforward ones, than I have. To get more in, I only put down the headings; if I added the sequel I would triple the volume. And how many stories have I scattered up and down this book that I only touch on — which anyone willing to look into them more curiously would find matter enough in them for an infinity of essays. Neither those stories nor my quotations always serve simply as example, authority, or ornament; I do not value them only for the use I put them to: they sometimes carry, beyond what I apply them to, the seed of richer and bolder matter, and sometimes, by the way, a more delicate resonance both for me — who will say nothing more about it here — and for others of my own bent.
But to come back to the speaking virtue: I see little to choose between knowing only how to speak ill and knowing only how to speak well.
"Non est ornamentum virile concinnitas."
["Carefully arranged dress is no manly ornament." — Seneca, Ep., 115.]
The sages tell us that, as regards knowledge, there is nothing except philosophy; and as regards conduct, nothing except virtue, which is universally suited to all degrees and all classes.

There is something like this in those other two philosophers, for they too promise immortality to the letters they write to their friends; but it is in another manner, and by adapting themselves, for a good end, to the vanity of another. For they tell them that, if concern about being known to future ages, and thirst for glory, still keeps them in public affairs and makes them afraid of the solitude and retirement to which they would persuade them, then they need not trouble themselves any more about it, since they will have enough credit with posterity to ensure that, even if there were nothing else, the letters thus written to them will make their names as known and famous as their own public actions could. And, besides this difference, these are not idle, empty letters that contain nothing but a fine jingle of well-chosen words and delicately turned phrases, but ones full and packed with great reasonings, by which a man may become not more eloquent but wiser — letters that teach us not to speak but to do well. Away with that eloquence that enchants us with itself, not with real things — unless you will allow Cicero's to be of so supreme a perfection that it forms a complete body in itself.

I will add one more story we read of him to this purpose, in which his nature will be laid open to us much more plainly. He was to deliver a speech in public and found himself a little pressed for time to get himself ready at his ease; when Eros, one of his slaves, brought him word that the audience had been put off until the next day, he was so overcome with joy that he gave the man his freedom for the good news.

On the subject of letters, I will add this to what has been said: it is a kind of writing in which my friends think I can do something; and I am willing to confess that I would have preferred to publish my whimsies in that form than in any other, had I had someone to write to. But I lacked the kind of settled correspondence I once had — one that would draw me to it, raise my fancy, and sustain me. As for trafficking with the wind, as some others have done, and forging imaginary names to address letters to, on a serious subject — I could only ever do this in a dream, being a sworn enemy of every kind of falsification. I should have been more diligent and more confident if I had had a judicious and indulgent friend to address, rather than exposing myself like this to the various judgments of a whole public; and I am much mistaken if I would not have done better that way. I have naturally a humorous and familiar style; but it is a style of my own, not fit for public business — like the language I speak, too compact, irregular, abrupt, idiosyncratic. As for letters of ceremony that have no substance beyond a polite weaving of courteous words, I am hopelessly at a loss; I have neither faculty nor taste for those tedious offerings of service and affection; I believe little of them from others, and I would not forgive myself for saying to others more than I myself believe. This is, no doubt, very far from current practice; for there has never been so abject and servile a prostitution of offers: life, soul, devotion, adoration, vassal, slave, and I can't tell what else — all such expressions so commonly and indifferently bandied about by everyone to everyone, that when they want to declare a greater and more respectful inclination on more deserving occasions, they have nothing left to express it with. I have a deep loathing of any whiff of flattery, which is why I naturally drop into a shy, rough, blunt way of speaking which, to those who do not know me, may seem to smack a little of disdain. I honour most those to whom I show the least honour, and where my soul moves with the greatest cheerfulness I easily forget the ceremonies of look and gesture, and offer myself faintly and bluntly to those to whom I am most devoted — they should, I think, read it in my heart; and the wording of what I say only injures the love I have inwardly conceived. As for welcoming, taking leave, giving thanks, accosting, offering one's services, and all those verbal formalities that the ceremonious laws of our modern civility prescribe, I know no one as stupidly unfurnished with such language as myself; and I have never been employed in writing letters of favour or recommendation without the man for whom they were written thinking my intervention cold and inadequate. The Italians are great printers of letters; I believe I have at least a hundred separate volumes of them, of which Annibale Caro's seem to me the best. If all the paper I have scribbled to the ladies, back when my hand was really prompted by passion, were still in existence, perhaps one might find a page worthy to be passed on to our young men in love, who are bewildered by that fury. I always write my letters at top speed — so headlong that, though I write quite illegibly, I would rather do it myself than employ another, since I can find no one able to keep up with me; and I never copy any out again. I have got the great ones who know me used to enduring my blots and crossings out, and to paper without fold or margin. The letters that cost me the most pains are the worst; when I begin dragging it along by the ears, it's a sign that I am not really in it. I throw myself in without forethought or design; the first word starts the second, and so on to the end of the chapter. The letters of this age consist more in fine edges and prefaces than in matter. Just as I would rather write two letters than fold and seal one (and always give that job to someone else), so, when the real business of my letter is finished, I would gladly hand it on to another to add those long harangues, offers, and prayers we put at the bottom — and I would be glad if some new custom would relieve us of that trouble; likewise of heading them with a long string of qualities and titles, which, for fear of mistakes, I have often left out altogether, especially to men of the long robe and of finance. There are so many new offices, such a shuffling and arranging of titles of honour, that it is hard to get them right; and yet, since they are so dearly bought, they cannot be altered or omitted without giving offence. I find it equally in bad taste to clutter the fronts and inscriptions of the books we send to the press with the like.

title: That the relish for good and evil depends in great measure upon the opinion we have of them
paragraphs: Men, says an ancient Greek maxim, are tormented by the opinions they have of things, not by the things themselves. It would be a great victory for the relief of our miserable human condition if this proposition could be established as certainly and universally true. For if evils only get into us by way of the judgment we ourselves make of them, it seems we have it in our own power to despise them or to turn them to good. If things surrender themselves to our mercy, why don't we convert them and put them to our advantage? If what we call evil and torment is neither evil nor torment in itself, but only takes on that quality because our imagination gives it to them, then we have it in us to change it; and since the choice lies with us, with no constraint forced on us, we must be very strange fools to take up arms on the side that hurts us most, and to give sickness, want, and contempt a bitter and nauseating taste, when it is in our power to give them a pleasant one — if fortune merely supplies the matter, leaving the form to us. Now, that what we call evil is not so in itself, or at least not to the degree we make it, and that we have it in us to give it another taste and complexion (all of which amounts to the same thing), let us examine how that case can be made.

If the original being of the things we fear had the power to lodge itself in us by its own authority, it would lodge itself in everyone alike, in the same way; for men are all of the same kind, and apart from differences in degree, are all furnished with the same instruments for conceiving and judging. But the diversity of opinions we hold about these things makes it perfectly plain that they only enter us through some compromise: one person, perhaps, admits them as they truly are, but a thousand others give them a new and contrary being inside themselves. We treat death, poverty, and pain as our chief enemies. Now this death, which some take to be the most dreadful of all dreadful things — who doesn't know that others call it the only safe harbour from the storms and tempests of life, the supreme good in nature, the sole support of liberty, and the common, ready-to-hand remedy for all evils? And while some wait for it with fear and trembling, others put up with it more easily than with life. One man complains that it comes too easily:
"Mors! utinam pavidos vitae subducere nolles. Sed virtus to sola daret!"
["O death! would that you might refuse to spare the coward, and that valour alone could pay you tribute." — Lucan, iv. 580.]

Leaving these boastful courages aside: Theodorus, when Lysimachus threatened to kill him, answered, "You'll do a brave deed indeed — to match the strength of a blister-fly." The majority of philosophers, by all accounts, either deliberately anticipated their own death or hurried and helped it along. And how many ordinary people do we see led off to execution — not just to a simple death, but to one mixed with shame and sometimes with grievous tortures — and going with such assurance, whether out of firm courage or sheer natural simplicity, that you can see no change in them from their everyday selves? They settle their household affairs, commend themselves to friends, sing, preach, address the crowd, even break out into jokes and drink to their companions, quite as composedly as Socrates did.

One man being led to the gallows told his guards they must not take him through such-and-such a street, in case a merchant who lived there should stop him on the way over an old debt. Another told the hangman not to touch his neck because he was ticklish and would burst out laughing. Another, told by his confessor that he would sup with our Lord that very day, said, "You go in my place; I myself am fasting today." Another, having called for a drink, when the hangman drank first, said he would not drink after him for fear of catching some disease. Everyone has heard the tale of the Picard, who, standing on the ladder, was offered a common wench — the law sometimes allowing this — being told that if he would marry her his life would be spared. He looked her over for a while, noticed that she limped, and said, "Come on, string me up, string me up; she limps." They tell a similar story of a man in Denmark, condemned to lose his head, who was offered the same bargain on the scaffold and refused, because the girl on offer had hollow cheeks and too sharp a nose. A servant in Toulouse, accused of heresy, when asked what he believed referred himself to the belief of his master, a young student who was a fellow prisoner, choosing rather to die than allow himself to be persuaded that his master could be wrong. We read that when Louis XI took the city of Arras, a great many of its inhabitants let themselves be hanged rather than say "God save the King." And even among that mean-souled tribe, the buffoons, there have been some who would not stop fooling around at the very moment of death. One, as the hangman was launching him off the ladder, cried out "Launch the galley!" — one of his stock sayings. Another, lying at the point of death on a bed of straw set before the fire by his friends, was asked by the doctor where the pain lay. "Between the bench and the fire," he said. When the priest, coming to give him extreme unction, was groping for his feet — which the pain had made him pull up under him — he said, "You'll find them at the end of my legs." To someone present urging him to commend himself to God, he said, "Why, who's going there?" — and the man replied, "You will be presently, if such is His pleasure." "Am I sure to be there by tomorrow night?" he asked. "Just commend yourself to Him," the other said, "and you'll be there soon enough." "Then I'd best," said he, "carry my own recommendations."

In the kingdom of Narsingah to this day the wives of priests are buried alive with their husbands' corpses; all other wives are burned at their husbands' funerals, which they undergo not just firmly but cheerfully. When the king dies, his wives and concubines, his favourites, all his officers and household servants — a whole population — present themselves so gaily at the fire where his body is burned, that they seem to take it as a singular honour to accompany their master in death. During our recent wars in Milan, with so many takings and retakings of towns, the people grew so impatient with the swings of fortune that they resolved on death; I have heard my father say that he there saw a list drawn up of twenty-five heads of households who killed themselves in the course of a single week. It is reminiscent of what happened with the Xanthians, besieged by Brutus, when men, women, and children fell into such a furious appetite for dying that there was nothing they wouldn't do to avoid life, and Brutus had great trouble saving even a small number of them.

Any opinion is powerful enough to get itself adopted at the cost of life. The first article of that brave oath which Greece swore and kept in the Median war was that every man would sooner exchange his life for death than exchange his own laws for those of Persia. In the wars between the Turks and the Greeks, what crowds of people do we see preferring a cruel death to un-circumcising themselves and accepting baptism? An example to which no religion is immune.

When the kings of Castile banished the Jews from their lands, John, King of Portugal, in return for eight crowns a head, sold them refuge in his own kingdom for a limited period, on condition that when the period expired they were to leave, and he would furnish ships to transport them to Africa. The day came, and they were given to understand that any who remained in the kingdom afterwards would become slaves; the vessels provided were poorly equipped; and those who embarked were treated brutally and shamefully by the crews, who, among other indignities, kept them crisscrossing at sea — now forward, now back — until they had used up all their provisions and were forced to buy more from the sailors at extortionate prices for so long that they were not set on shore until they had been stripped to their very shirts. When news of this inhuman treatment reached those who had remained behind, the greater part of them resolved to accept slavery; some made a show of converting. Emmanuel, John's successor, on coming to the throne first set them at liberty, then changed his mind and ordered them out of the country, assigning three ports for their departure. He hoped, says Bishop Osorius — no contemptible Latin historian of these recent times — that since the favour of liberty he had granted them had failed to convert them to Christianity, the difficulty of trusting themselves to the mercy of the sailors and of abandoning a country in which they were now settled and had grown rich, in order to expose themselves in strange and unknown regions, would at last do it. But, finding himself mistaken in this expectation, and that they were all resolved on the voyage, he cut off two of the three ports he had promised them, so that the length and discomfort of the passage might reduce some to compliance — or that he might, by squeezing them all into one place, more conveniently carry out what he had designed: which was to seize every child under fourteen from the arms of their fathers and mothers, transporting them out of sight and contact, into a place where they could be instructed and brought up in our religion. He says this produced a most horrid spectacle. The natural affection between parents and children, and beyond that their zeal for their ancient belief, fighting against this violent decree, fathers and mothers were commonly seen killing themselves; and, by a still more terrible example, throwing their own young children into wells and pits out of love and compassion, to escape the severity of the law. As for the rest, when the appointed time expired, for lack of means to transport them they fell back into slavery. Some also turned Christian, but on whose faith — and on that of their descendants, even today, a hundred years on — few Portuguese yet feel they can rely; though custom and length of time are far more powerful counsellors in such changes than any other constraint. In the town of Castelnaudari, fifty heretic Albigensians let themselves be burned alive in a single fire rather than renounce their views.
"Quoties non modo ductores nostri, sed universi etiam exercitus, ad non dubiam mortem concurrerunt?"
["How often have not only our leaders, but whole armies, run to certain and manifest death." — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., i. 37.]

I have seen a close friend of mine run headlong upon death with real affection — a passion rooted in his heart by various plausible arguments which he would never let me dislodge — and, at the first honourable occasion that offered, throw himself into it without any visible motive, with an obstinate and ardent desire of dying. We have several examples in our own day of people, even young children, who, to escape some small inconvenience, have done away with themselves. And what shall we not fear, says one of the ancients on this subject, if we dread the thing that cowardice itself has chosen as its refuge?

If I were to draw up a long catalogue here of all those, of every sex, condition, and sect, even in the happiest ages, who have either with great steadiness looked death in the face or voluntarily sought it out — sought it out not only to escape the evils of this life, but some purely to escape the satiety of living, and others in hope of a better state elsewhere — I should never finish. Indeed, the number is so vast that I should do better to count up those who have feared it. One example will serve for all: Pyrrho the philosopher, finding himself one day in a boat in a violent storm, pointed out to those whom he saw most terrified, by way of encouragement, a pig that was on board, perfectly unconcerned. Shall we then dare to claim that this advantage of reason, of which we boast so much, on the strength of which we suppose ourselves masters and emperors over the rest of creation, was given to us as a torment? What good is the knowledge of things if it leaves us less manly? if we lose by it the tranquillity and repose we would enjoy without it? if it puts us in a worse state than Pyrrho's pig? Shall we put the understanding that was conferred on us for our greatest good to our own ruin, setting ourselves against the design of nature and the universal order of things — which means every creature to make use of the faculties, members, and means it has, to its own best advantage?

But it may be objected against me: "Your rule holds well enough as to death; but what will you say about poverty? What, moreover, about pain — which Aristippus, Hieronymus, and most of the sages have reputed the worst of all evils; and which even those who have denied it in words have admitted in their conduct? Posidonius, racked with a sharp and painful disease, was visited by Pompey, who apologised for having come at such a bad moment to hear him discourse on philosophy. "The gods forbid," said Posidonius, "that pain should ever have the power to stop me from talking," and at once launched into a discourse on the contempt of pain — while all the while his own infirmity was playing its part and tormenting him properly. To which he cried out, "Do your worst, pain, work me over with all your power, but you'll never make me say you are an evil." This story they make such a fuss about — what, I'd like to know, does it really have to do with the contempt of pain? He's only fighting it with words; in the meantime, if the shootings and stabs he felt did not move him, why did he interrupt his discourse? Why did he think he was doing such a great thing in refusing to call it an evil? Not everything here is in the imagination; our fancies may operate on other things, but here it's certain knowledge that is at stake, of which our senses themselves are the judges:
"Qui nisi sunt veri, ratio quoque falsa sit omnis."
["If they are not true, then all reasoning may also be false." — Lucretius, iv. 486.]

Shall we convince our skin that the cracks of a whip pleasantly tickle us, or our taste that a dose of aloes is vin de Graves? Pyrrho's pig is in the same predicament as we are; it's true he isn't afraid of death, but if you beat him he'll squeal to some purpose. Shall we force the general law of nature, which we see in every living creature under heaven, to tremble under pain? Even the trees seem to groan under the blows they take. Death is felt only by reason, since it is the motion of an instant:
