"Aut fuit, aut veniet; nihil est praesentis in illa."
["It has been, or it will come: there is nothing of the present in it." — Estienne de la Boétie, Satires.]
"Morsque minus poenae, quam mora mortis, habet;"
["The delay of death is more painful than death itself." — Ovid, Ep. Ariadne to Theseus, v. 42.]
A thousand beasts, a thousand men, are dead sooner than threatened. What we mainly claim to fear in death is pain, its ordinary herald: yet if we may trust a holy father:
"Malam mortem non facit, nisi quod sequitur mortem."
["It is what follows death that makes death bad." — St. Augustine, De Civit. Dei, i. ii.]
And I should say, more probably still, that neither what goes before nor what comes after is any part of death itself.

We excuse ourselves falsely; I find by experience that it is rather the impatience of the imagination of death that makes us impatient of pain, and we find pain doubly grievous because it threatens us with death. But because reason accuses our cowardice for fearing a thing so sudden, so inevitable, and so unfelt, we take the other as the more excusable pretext. All ills that carry no other danger with them but the evils themselves we treat as things of no danger: toothache and gout, painful as they are, are not reckoned mortal, so who counts them among the diseases?

But let us grant that in death our chief concern is the pain — just as in poverty there is nothing to fear except the miseries it brings of thirst, hunger, cold, heat, sleepless nights, and the other discomforts it makes us suffer — still, all we have to deal with is pain. I will grant, and very willingly, that it is the worst incident of our being (I am the man on earth who most hates and avoids it, given that thus far, thank God, I have had so little business with it). But it is still in us, if not to abolish it, at least to lessen it by patience; and even if body and reason mutiny, to keep the soul in good condition. If this were not so, who would ever have given a reputation to virtue, valour, force, magnanimity, resolution? Where would they have a part to play if there were no pain to defy?
"Avida est periculi virtus."
["Courage is greedy of danger." — Seneca, De Providentia, c. 4.]

Without lying on the bare ground, without enduring in full armour the midday heat, without feeding on the flesh of horses and asses, without seeing oneself hacked to pieces, without suffering a bullet to be pulled out from among shattered bones, without the sewing up, cauterising, and probing of wounds — by what means is the advantage we covet over the common run of men to be acquired? Far from fleeing evil and pain, the sages tell us that among equally good actions a man should prefer to perform the one that involves greater effort and pain.
"Non est enim hilaritate, nec lascivia, nec risu, aut joco comite levitatis, sed saepe etiam tristes firmitate et constantia sunt beati."

["For men are not only made happy by mirth and wantonness, by laughter and jesting, the companion of levity, but often the serious sort reap happiness from their firmness and constancy." — Cicero, De Finib. ii. 10.]

For this reason it has always been impossible to persuade our forefathers that victories obtained by force and at the hazard of war were not more honourable than those secured safely by stratagem or trick:
"Laetius est, quoties magno sibi constat honestum."
["A good deed is all the more satisfying the more it has cost us." — Lucan, ix. 404.]
Besides, this ought to be a comfort: that naturally, if the pain is violent it is short; and if it is long, it is not violent.
"Si gravis, brevis; Si longus, levis."
You will not feel it for long if you feel it too much: it will either put an end to itself or to you; it comes to the same thing. If you cannot bear it, it will carry you off:

["Remember that the greatest pains are ended by death; that lighter pains have long intervals of rest, and that we are masters of the more moderate sort: so that if they are bearable, we bear them; if not, we can leave life, as we leave a theatre, when it ceases to please." — Cicero, De Finib. i. 15.]

What makes us suffer pain so impatiently is that we are not used to settling our chief contentment in the soul, and that we don't rely enough on her who is the sole and sovereign mistress of our condition. The body, give or take in degree, has only one and the same bent; whereas the soul is variable into every sort of shape, and subject to her own command are all things — the senses of the body and every other accident. That is why we ought to study her, to question her, and to rouse up all her powerful faculties. There is neither reason, force, nor injunction that can prevail against her inclination and choice. Of the many thousand biases at her disposal, let us give her one fitted to our peace and conversation, and we shall not only be sheltered and secured from all manner of injury and offence, but, if she so wills, actually gratified and obliged by evils and offences. She turns everything to her own profit; error, dreams, serve her purposes well, as good material for lodging us in safety and contentment. It is plain enough to see that it is the sharpness of our mind that gives the edge to our pains and our pleasures. Beasts, having no such thing, leave their bodies to their own free and natural feelings, and accordingly in every species these are about the same, as their similar motions show. If we did not interfere with our limbs in the jurisdiction that belongs to them in this, we would probably be better off; nature has given them a fair and moderate temper for both pleasure and pain, and this temper cannot fail to be just, being equal and common. But since we have freed ourselves from her rules to give ourselves up to the rambling liberty of our own fancies, let us at least help to bend them to the more agreeable side. Plato fears our engaging ourselves too strongly with pain and pleasure, on the grounds that they too much knit and ally the soul to the body; I, on the contrary, think it is rather that they separate and disunite them too much. As an enemy is made fiercer by our flight, so pain grows proud at seeing us cringe under it. It will surrender on much better terms to those who stand up to it; a man must oppose it and stoutly set himself against it. In retreating and giving ground, we invite and bring upon ourselves the ruin that threatens us. As the body is firmer in an encounter the more stiffly and obstinately it applies itself to it, so it is with the soul.

But let us come to examples — the proper sport of folks as feebly equipped as I am — where we shall find that it is with pain as with stones, which take a brighter or duller lustre depending on the setting they are put in, and that it has no more room in us than we choose to allow it:
"Tantum doluerunt, quantum doloribus se inseruerunt."
["They suffered the more, the more they gave way to suffering." — St. Augustine, De Civit. Dei, i. 10.]

We are more sensitive to one little touch of a surgeon's lancet than to twenty sword-wounds in the heat of a fight. The pains of childbirth, said by the physicians and by God himself to be great, and which we surround with so many ceremonies — there are whole nations that think nothing of them. I'll leave the Spartan women aside, but what else do you find among the Swiss in our own infantry, when, trotting along after their husbands, you see them today carrying at their necks the child they carried yesterday in their bellies? The so-called Gypsies among us go and wash theirs themselves as soon as they come into the world, bathing them in the first river they meet. Beyond the many girls who daily drop their babies on the sly, as quietly as they conceived them, that noble and beautiful wife of Sabinus, a Roman patrician, endured for another's sake, alone, without help, without crying out, without so much as a groan, the birth of twins. A poor simple boy of Sparta, having stolen a fox (they fear the shame of stupidity in stealing more than we fear the punishment for the theft itself), having got it under his coat, let it tear out his guts rather than reveal the theft. And another, offering incense at a sacrifice, let himself be burned to the bone by a coal that fell into his sleeve, rather than disturb the ceremony. And there have been a great number who, for a sole test of virtue and in keeping with their institutions, endured at seven years old to be whipped to death without changing their expression. And Cicero saw them fight in teams, with fists, feet, and teeth, until they fainted and fell, rather than admit themselves beaten:

["Custom could never conquer nature; she is always invincible; but we have infected the mind with shadows, delights, negligence, sloth; we have grown soft through opinions and corrupt morality." — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., v. 27.]

Everyone knows the story of Scaevola, who slipped into the enemy camp to kill their general, missed his stroke, and to retrieve his blunder by a still stranger device and free his country, boldly confessed to Porsenna — the king he had meant to kill — not only his plan, but added that there were then a great number of Romans in the camp, his accomplices in the enterprise, as good men as he. To show what kind of man he himself was, he called for a pan of burning coals to be brought and watched and endured his arm being broiled and roasted, until the king himself, horrified at the sight, ordered the pan to be taken away. What would you say of the man who refused to interrupt his reading even while he was being cut into? Or of the other one, who kept mocking and laughing in contempt of the pains inflicted on him, so that the provoked cruelty of the executioners in charge of him, and all the inventions of torture redoubled on him one after another, were spent in vain and at last had to give him best? But he was a philosopher. Well then — a gladiator of Caesar's endured, laughing all the while, his wounds being probed, lanced, and laid open:

["What ordinary gladiator ever groaned? Which of them ever changed countenance? Which of them stood or fell without dignity? Which, having fallen and being commanded to receive the sword-stroke, drew in his neck?" — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., ii. 17.]

Let us bring in the women too. Who in Paris has not heard of the woman who had her face flayed for the sake of a fresher complexion under new skin? There are those who have pulled out good sound teeth to make their voices softer and sweeter, or to set the other teeth in better order. How many examples of contempt of pain do we have in that sex? What won't they do, what won't they undertake, for the smallest hope of adding to their beauty?
"Vallere queis cura est albos a stirpe capillos, Et faciem, dempta pelle, referre novam."
["Who carefully pluck out their grey hairs by the roots, and renew their faces by peeling off the old skin." — Tibullus, i. 8, 45.]

I have seen some of them swallow sand and ashes, and do their utmost to wreck their stomachs to get pale complexions. To shape a fine Spanish figure, what tortures of girding and lacing won't they endure, till they have notches cut into their sides to the very quick, and sometimes to death?

It is a common thing in several nations today to wound themselves in earnest as proof of their faith; our king relates notable examples of what he has seen in Poland and done to himself. But besides this, which I know to have been imitated by some in France, a little before I came from that famous assembly of the Estates at Blois I had seen a girl in Picardy who, to demonstrate the ardour of her promises and her constancy, gave herself, with a hairpin she wore in her hair, four or five good hearty stabs in the arm, until the blood gushed out freely. The Turks give themselves great scars in honour of their mistresses, and, to make them last longer, they at once clap fire to the wound, holding it there for an incredible time to stop the bleeding and form the scar; people who have been eyewitnesses have both written and sworn this to me. But for ten aspers there you can find fellows any day who will give themselves a good deep slash in the arm or thigh. I prefer, however, to have testimonies from closer to home when we have most need of them: Christendom supplies us with plenty. After the example of our blessed Saviour there have been many who have crucified themselves. We have evidence very worthy of belief that King St. Louis wore a hair shirt until in his old age his confessor gave him a dispensation to leave it off; and that every Friday he had his shoulders flogged by his priest with five small iron chains, which were always carried among his bedtime equipment for that purpose.

William, our last Duke of Guienne, the father of that Eleanor who carried the duchy into the houses of France and England, wore continuously for the last ten or twelve years of his life a suit of armour under a religious habit, by way of penance. Foulke, Count of Anjou, went all the way to Jerusalem to have himself whipped there by two of his servants, with a rope around his neck, before the sepulchre of our Lord. But don't we still, every Good Friday in various places, see great numbers of men and women beating and whipping themselves until they tear and cut the flesh to the very bone? I have often seen it, and without any trick to it; and it was said that there were some among them (they go disguised) who for money undertook by this means to bear the religious penance of others, by a contempt of pain all the greater because the incentives of devotion are more powerful than those of greed. Q. Maximus buried his son when he was consul, M. Cato his when praetor-elect, and L. Paulus both of his within a few days of each other, all of them with a countenance that showed no kind of grief. I once said jokingly of a certain man that he had cheated divine justice; for the violent death of three of his grown children was sent to him on a single day, as a severe scourge, presumably; and so far from being afflicted by it, he took it for a particular grace and favour of heaven. I do not go in for these monstrous humours, although I lost two or three children at nurse, if not without grief at least without complaint, and there is hardly an accident that cuts closer to the quick. I see many other grounds of sorrow that, if they happened to me, I would barely feel; and I have despised some, when they have come on me, to which the world has given so terrible a figure that I would blush to boast of my equanimity.
"Ex quo intelligitur, non in natura, sed in opinione, esse aegritudinem."
["From which one may understand that grief is not in nature, but in opinion." — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., iii. 28.]

Opinion is a powerful party, bold, and immoderate. Who ever chased after security and ease as greedily as Alexander and Caesar chased after disturbance and difficulty? Teres, the father of Sitalces, used to say that when he had no wars on, he felt there was no difference between himself and his groom. Cato the consul, in order to secure some cities in Spain from revolt, did nothing but forbid the inhabitants to carry weapons, and a great many of them killed themselves:
"Ferox gens, nullam vitam rati sine armis esse."
["A fierce people, who thought there was no life without war." — Livy, xxxiv. 17.]

How many do we know who have abandoned the calm and sweetness of a quiet life at home among their acquaintances, to seek out the horror of uninhabitable deserts, and having flung themselves into so abject a state as to become the scorn and contempt of the world, have hugged themselves at the idea, even to the point of affectation? Cardinal Borromeo, who recently died at Milan, in the midst of all the merriment that the climate of Italy, his youth, his birth, and his great wealth invited him to, kept to so austere a way of life that the same robe served him for summer and for winter; he had nothing but straw for his bed, and the leisure hours he had between business he spent continually on his knees in study, with a little bread and a glass of water set beside his book — and that was all his meal, and all the time he gave to eating.
I know some who have consentingly drawn both profit and advancement from cuckoldry, the very name of which terrifies so many people.

If sight is not the most necessary of all our senses, it is at least the most pleasant; but the most pleasant and most useful of all our members seem to be those of generation — and yet a great many people have conceived a deadly hatred against them precisely because they were too pleasant, and have done away with them just because they valued them so much, like the man who put out his own eyes. Most people, and the more solid sort, look on an abundance of children as a great blessing; I and some others think it just as great a benefit to be without them. And when you ask Thales why he doesn't marry, he tells you it's because he doesn't care to leave any posterity behind him.

That it is our opinion that gives things their value is clear enough from the great number of things which we prize, not so much for themselves as for ourselves, never reckoning either their virtues or their use, but only how dearly they cost us — as if that were part of their substance — so that the only value we set on them is not what they bring us but what we put into them. From which I gather that we are great economists of our own expense: it counts for as much as it weighs. Our opinion will never let it want for value: price gives value to the diamond, difficulty to virtue, suffering to devotion, bitterness to medicine. A certain man, to make himself poor, threw his crowns into the very sea where so many come, from all parts of the world, to fish for riches. Epicurus says that being rich is no relief, only an alteration, of one's circumstances. In truth, it is not want, but abundance, that breeds greed. Let me share my own experience on this point.

Ever since I emerged from childhood I have lived in three different conditions. The first, which lasted some twenty years, I passed without any income except what was occasional and dependent on the allowance and assistance of others, generous but unsteady. I spent my money all the more cheerfully, and with all the less care for how it went, since it depended entirely on my over-confidence in fortune. I never lived more at ease; I never had the rebuff of finding the purse of any friend shut against me, having imposed on myself this necessity above all others: never to default on payment at the agreed time, even though they themselves a thousand times put it off, seeing how careful I was to satisfy them — so I practised a thrift that was at the same time a kind of charming honesty. I feel a natural pleasure in paying, as though I were lifting a tiresome weight off my shoulders and freeing myself from an image of slavery; and I also find a kind of ravishing satisfaction in pleasing another and doing a just act. I except payments that involve haggling and reckoning; in such cases, when I can find nobody to take that burden off me, I postpone them, as scandalously and inexcusably as you like, as long as I can, out of fear of those wranglings for which both my temperament and my way of speaking are entirely unsuited. There is nothing I hate so much as driving a bargain; it's a sheer business of trickery and shamelessness, where after an hour of haggling and hesitating both sides abandon their word and their oath for the sake of a five-sou discount. Still, I always borrowed at a disadvantage, since, lacking the confidence to speak in person, I would entrust my request to a letter, which is usually a poor advocate and gives the man inclined to refuse every opening. I was then more cheerfully and freely committing the conduct of my affairs to the stars than I have since done to my own management and judgment. Most good economists regard it as a horrible thing to live always in such uncertainty, and don't consider, first, that the greatest part of the world lives that way: how many worthy men have wholly let go of their own certainties, and still do every day, to trust to the inconstant favour of princes and of fortune? Caesar ran over a million in gold into debt, beyond what he was worth, to become Caesar; and how many merchants have begun their trade by selling off their farms to send the proceeds to the Indies,
"Tot per impotentia freta."
["Through so many ungovernable seas." — Catullus, iv. 18.]

In so great a drought of devotion as we see these days, we have a thousand and a thousand colleges that get along comfortably enough, expecting their dinner each day from the generosity of Heaven. Second, they don't notice that the certainty they rely on so heavily is not much less uncertain and hazardous than chance itself. I see misery just as close at hand on two thousand crowns a year as if it stood next to me; for besides the fact that chance can make a hundred breaches into poverty through the strongest walls of our riches — there is very often no middle ground between the highest and the lowest fortune:
"Fortuna vitrea est: turn, quum splendet, frangitur,"
["Fortune is glass: in its greatest brilliance it breaks." — From the Mims of P. Syrus.]

And, to turn all our barricades and bulwarks upside down, I find that, from various causes, poverty is as often seen to lodge with those who have estates as with those who have none; and perhaps it is then far less grievous when alone than when accompanied by riches. These flow more from good management than from revenue:
"Faber est suae quisque fortunae"
["Each man is the maker of his own fortune." — Sallust, De Repub. Ord., i. 1.]
And an uneasy, needy, busy rich man seems to me more miserable than the man who is simply poor.
"In divitiis inopes, quod genus egestatis gravissimum est."
["Poor in the midst of riches, which is the worst kind of poverty." — Seneca, Ep., 74.]

The greatest and wealthiest princes are driven by poverty and want to the most extreme necessity; for can there be any more extreme than to become tyrants and unjust usurpers of their subjects' goods and estates?

My second condition of life was to have money of my own; I managed things so that I soon laid up a considerable sum out of a modest fortune, on the principle that what one really owns is what one sets aside out of one's ordinary spending, and that one cannot absolutely rely on revenue one only hopes to receive, however clear the hope may be. "For what," I said, "if I should be caught short by some accident?" And after such empty and vicious imaginings, I would very wisely, by this hoarding, provide against all eventualities; and could, moreover, answer those who objected that the number of these was too vast that, if I couldn't lay up for all, I could at least do it for some, and for many. Yet this was not done without a great deal of solicitude and anxiety. I kept it very close, and though I dare to talk so boldly about myself, I never spoke truly of my money — but falsely, as others do, who being rich pretend to be poor, and being poor pretend to be rich, dispensing their consciences from ever telling sincerely what they have: a ridiculous and shameful prudence. Was I going on a journey? It seemed to me I was never well enough provided; and the more I loaded myself with money, the more I loaded myself with fear — one moment about the danger of the roads, the next about the loyalty of the man in charge of my baggage; of whom, like some others I know, I was never sufficiently sure unless I kept him constantly in view. If I happened to leave my cash-box behind, oh, what strange suspicions and anxieties I fell into, and, what was worse, without daring to share them with anybody. My mind was eternally taken up with such things; so that, all in all, there is more trouble in keeping money than in earning it. And even if I didn't really do all I say, or wasn't really as ridiculously anxious about my money as I've made out, it still cost me something at least to restrain myself from being so. I drew little or no advantage from what I had, and my expenses seemed no less to me for having more to spend; for, as Bion said, hairy men are as angry as bald men at being plucked. Once you are used to it and have set your heart on your hoard, it is no longer at your service: you can't bring yourself to break into it. It's like a building you fancy must inevitably collapse to ruin if you so much as stir a single pebble; necessity must take you by the throat before you will bring yourself to touch it. I would sooner have pawned anything I owned, or sold a horse, and with much less reluctance, than have made the slightest breach in that beloved purse I had so carefully laid by. But the danger is that a man cannot easily set certain limits to this desire (they are hard to find for things one takes to be good), and to hold this good husbandry short of degenerating into miserliness. People are forever intent on adding to the heap, and increasing the stock from sum to sum, until at last they vilely deprive themselves of the enjoyment of their own goods, and put everything in reserve without making any use of it at all. By this rule the richest people in the world are those set to guard the walls and gates of a wealthy city. All money-men, I conclude, are misers. Plato sets out the corporal or human goods in this order: health, beauty, strength, riches; and riches, he says, are not blind, but very clear-sighted, when illuminated by prudence. Dionysius the Younger did a very fine thing on this subject; he was informed that one of his Syracusans had hidden a treasure in the ground, and sent word for him to bring it. The man brought it, secretly keeping back only a small part for himself, with which he went off to another city, where, having been cured of his appetite for hoarding, he began to live in a more liberal style. When Dionysius heard of it, he had the rest of the treasure returned to him, saying that since the man had learned to use it, he was very willing to give it back.

I went on for some years in this hoarding humour, until some unknown good demon fortunately got me out of it, as it had the Syracusan, and made me throw all my reserves to the winds. The pleasure of a certain journey I took at great expense made me kick this foolish love of money underfoot, and by this means I have fallen into a third way of living (I'm telling you what I think of it) which is far more pleasant and regular: I live at the height of my revenue; sometimes one, sometimes the other may exceed, but only by a little and only rarely do they differ. I live from hand to mouth, and content myself with having enough for my present and ordinary expenses; for as to extraordinary occasions, all the saving up in the world would never be enough. And it's the greatest folly imaginable to expect that fortune should ever sufficiently arm us against herself; it's with our own weapons that we have to fight her; outside ones will betray us in the pinch. If I save, it's for some near and specific purpose, not to buy lands of which I have no need, but to buy pleasure:
"Non esse cupidum, pecunia est; non esse emacem, vertigal est."
["Not to be covetous is money; not to be acquisitive is revenue." — Cicero, Paradox., vi. 3.]
I am neither in any great fear of being in want nor desire any more:
"Divitiarum fructus est in copia; copiam declarat satietas."
["The fruit of riches is in abundance; satiety declares abundance." — Cicero, ibid., vi. 2.]

And I am very glad that this reformation in me has come about in an age that is naturally inclined toward greed, and that I see myself clear of a folly so common to old men, and the most ridiculous of all human follies.

Feraulez, a man who had gone through both fortunes, and found that the increase of property was no increase of appetite — whether for eating, drinking, sleeping, or the enjoyment of his wife — and who on the other hand felt the care of his economics weighing heavily on his shoulders, as it does on mine, decided to do a favour to a poor young man, his loyal friend, who hankered after wealth; and made him a gift of all that he had, which was excessively great, and moreover of all he was going to receive day by day from the generosity of Cyrus, his good master, and from the war, on condition that he would handsomely maintain him and entertain him liberally as his guest and friend. This being done accordingly, they afterwards lived very happily together, both of them equally content with the change of their condition. It is an example I could imitate with all my heart; and I very much approve of the fortune of the aged prelate whom I see to have so completely stripped himself of his purse, his revenue, and the care of his expenses, committing them now to one trusty servant, now to another, that he has spun out a long succession of years, by this means as ignorant of his domestic affairs as any stranger.

Confidence in another man's virtue is no light evidence of one's own, and God willingly favours such confidence. As for the man I am speaking of, I see nowhere a better-managed house, more nobly and steadily kept up than his. Happy is he to have ordered his affairs in such just proportion that his estate is enough to do it without his concern or trouble, and without any interference, either in the spending or the saving, with his other quieter occupations, more suitable both to his position and to his taste.
Plenty, then, and want depend upon the opinion each of us has of them; and riches no more than glory or health have any beauty or pleasure beyond what is lent to them by their possessor.

Each of us is well or ill at ease according as he finds himself; not he whom the world thinks so, but he who thinks himself so, is content; and in this alone does belief give itself reality and being. Fortune does us neither good nor harm; she only presents the matter and the seed, which our soul, more powerful than she, turns and applies as she pleases — the sole cause and sovereign mistress of her own happy or unhappy condition. All external accessions take their taste and colour from the internal constitution, just as clothes warm us not with their own heat but with ours, which they are fit to cover and nourish; and one who would warm a cold body with them would do the same service for the cold, since snow and ice are preserved by the same means. And just as study is a torment to an idle man, abstinence from wine to a drunkard, frugality to a spendthrift, and exercise to a lazy, soft-bred fellow, so it is with everything else. The things are not painful and difficult in themselves; it is our weakness or cowardice that makes them so. To judge of great and high matters requires a soul of corresponding quality; otherwise we attribute to them the vice that is really our own. A straight oar looks crooked in the water: it isn't enough that we see the thing; we have to ask how, and after what manner, we see it.

After all this, why, out of so many discourses that persuade men with so many arguments to despise death and bear pain, can't we find one that helps us? And out of so many sorts of imaginings as have prevailed on others to persuade them to do so, why doesn't every man apply some one of them to himself, the one best suited to his own temper? If he can't stomach a strong decoction to root out the evil, let him at least take a mild remedy to ease it:

["It is an effeminate and flimsy opinion, no more so in pain than in pleasure: when at our ease, we cannot bear without a cry the sting of a bee. The whole business is to be master of yourself." — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., ii. 22.]

As for the rest, a man does not transgress philosophy by allowing the sharpness of pain and human frailty to prevail beyond measure; for they drive her back to her unanswerable replies: "If it is bad to live in necessity, at least there is no necessity to live in necessity"; "No one is unhappy for long except by his own fault." Of the man who has neither the courage to die nor the heart to live, who will neither resist nor flee, what can be done?

title: Not to communicate a man's honour
paragraphs: Of all the follies of the world, the one most universally embraced is concern for reputation and glory; we are so fond of it that we abandon riches, peace, life, and health — which are real and substantial goods — to chase after this empty phantom of a word, with no body to it, no hold to take on it:
"La fama, ch'invaghisce a un dolce suono Gli superbi mortali, et par si bella, E un eco, un sogno, anzi d'un sogno un'ombra, Ch'ad ogni vento si dilegua a sgombra."

["Fame, which with sweet sound charms proud mortals and seems so fair, is but an echo, a dream — nay, the shadow of a dream — which at every breath of wind vanishes and dissolves." — Tasso, Gerus., xiv. 63.]

And of all the irrational humours of men, it would seem that the philosophers themselves are among the last and most reluctant to free themselves from this one; it's the most stubborn and obstinate of all:
"Quia etiam bene proficientes animos tentare non cessat."
["Because it does not cease to assail even well-directed minds." — St. Augustine, De Civit. Dei, v. 14.]

There is no folly whose vanity reason exposes more clearly; but it is so deeply rooted in us that I don't dare decide whether anyone has ever wholly cleared themselves of it. Even after you have said all and believed all that can be said against it, it produces such an inward inclination in opposition to your best arguments that you have little power to resist it. As Cicero says, even those who most argue against it would yet have the books they write on the subject appear under their own names, and seek to derive glory from seeming to despise it. Everything else is communicable and enters into commerce: we lend our goods and stake our lives for the needs and service of our friends; but to share one's honour, and dress another man in one's own glory, is very rarely seen.

And yet we have some examples of just that. Catulus Luctatius in the Cimbrian war, having done all he could to make his fleeing soldiers turn and face the enemy, finally fled with them himself, faking the coward, so that his men would look as though they were following their captain rather than running from the enemy — sacrificing his own reputation in order to cover the shame of others. When Charles V came into Provence in 1537, it is said that Antonio de Leva, seeing the emperor firmly resolved on the expedition and believing it would do him great honour, nevertheless very stiffly opposed it in council, so that the entire glory of the resolution would be attributed to his master, and it could be said his own wisdom and foresight were such that, against everyone else's opinion, he had brought about so great an enterprise — which was to do him honour at his own expense. The Thracian ambassadors, coming to console Archileonida, the mother of Brasidas, on the death of her son, and praising him to the point of saying he had left no equal behind him, she rejected this private and particular praise to attribute it to the public: "Don't tell me that," she said. "I know the city of Sparta has many citizens both greater and of greater worth than he." In the battle of Crécy, the Prince of Wales, then very young, had been given command of the vanguard; the brunt of the battle happened to fall in that part of the field, which led the lords with him, finding themselves overmatched, to send to King Edward to come up to their relief. He asked how his son was, and being told he was alive and on horseback: "Then I'd do him wrong," said the king, "to go and rob him of the honour of winning this battle he has sustained so long and so bravely. Whatever risk he runs, the honour shall be entirely his own." And accordingly he would neither come up himself nor send help, knowing that if he went, it would be said all would have been lost without his rescue, and the honour of the victory would be wholly given to him.
"Semper enim quod postremum adjectum est, id rem totam videtur traxisse."
["For that which is last added always seems to have accomplished the whole affair." — Livy, xxvii. 45.]

Many at Rome thought, and often said, that the greatest of Scipio's deeds were in part due to Laelius, whose constant practice it was always to advance and uphold Scipio's grandeur and renown without any care for his own. And Theopompus, king of Sparta, said to a man who told him the republic couldn't fail because he himself knew so well how to command: "It's rather," he replied, "because the people know so well how to obey." Just as women who succeeded to peerages had, despite their sex, the privilege of attending and voting in trials within the jurisdiction of the peers, so the ecclesiastical peers, despite their profession, were obliged to attend our kings in their wars, not just with their friends and servants but in person. The Bishop of Beauvais did so when he was with Philip Augustus at the battle of Bouvines, where he played a notable part in the action; but he didn't think it fitting for him to share in the fruit and glory of that violent and bloody trade. He took several of the enemy that day with his own hand and turned them over to the first gentleman he met, leaving it to him either to kill them or to accept their surrender, referring the whole execution to that other hand. He did this with the Earl of Salisbury, William, whom he handed over to Messire Jehan de Nesle. By a similar subtlety of conscience to the one I have just mentioned, he would kill but not wound, and so always fought with a mace. And a certain person of my own time, being reproached by the king for having laid hands on a priest, flatly and positively denied any such thing — meaning he had cudgelled and kicked him.

title: Of the inequality amongst us
paragraphs: Plutarch says somewhere that he does not find as great a difference between beast and beast as he does between man and man; which he says with reference to the inner qualities and perfections of the soul. And, in truth, I find so vast a distance between Epaminondas, by my reckoning of him, and certain people I know who are still men of good sense, that I'd willingly go beyond Plutarch and say there is more difference between such-and-such a man than between such a man and such a beast:
["Ah! how greatly one man may surpass another!" — Terence, Eunuchus, ii. 2.]

And that there are as many degrees of mind as there are cubits between us and heaven. But when it comes to estimating men, it's strange that, ourselves excepted, no other creature is valued beyond its own intrinsic qualities. We praise a horse for his strength and surefootedness,
"Volucrem Sic laudamus equum, facili cui plurima palma Fervet, et exsultat rauco victoria circo,"
["So we praise the swift horse, on whose easy mastery many a hand glows in applause, and victory exults in the hoarse circus." — Juvenal, viii. 57.]

and not for his rich trappings; a greyhound for his speed, not for his fine collar; a hawk for her wings, not for her jesses and bells. Why then, in the same way, don't we value a man for what is properly his own? He has a great retinue, a fine palace, so much credit, so many thousand pounds a year: all of that is about him, but not in him. You wouldn't buy a pig in a poke: if you're pricing a horse, you'll see him stripped of his housing-cloths, naked and open to your eye; or if he's clothed — as they used to be when presented to princes for sale — it'll be only on the less important parts, so that you may consider not so much the beauty of his colour or the breadth of his rump, but principally his legs, eyes, and feet, which are the parts of greatest use:
"Regibus hic mos est: ubi equos mercantur, opertos Inspiciunt; ne, si facies, ut saepe, decora Molli fulta pede est, emptorem inducat hiantem"

["This is the custom of kings: when they buy horses, they have them inspected uncovered, lest, if a handsome head (as often happens) is supported by a weak foot, it should tempt the gaping purchaser." — Horace, Sat., i. 2, 86.]

Why then, in giving your estimate of a man, do you size him up wrapped and muffled in his clothes? He shows you nothing but the parts that are not in the least his own, and conceals those by which alone you can really judge his worth. It's the price of the blade you want to know, not the price of the scabbard: you wouldn't perhaps bid a farthing for him, if you saw him stripped. You are to judge him by himself, not by what he wears; and, as one of the ancients neatly said: "Do you know why you reckon him tall? You're counting the height of his pattens." The pedestal is no part of the statue. Measure him without his stilts; let him lay aside his revenues and his titles; let him present himself in his shirt. Then look at whether his body is sound and lively, active and ready to perform its functions. What kind of soul has he? Is she beautiful, capable, and properly furnished with all her faculties? Is she rich in what is her own, or in what she has borrowed? Has fortune had any hand in the business? Can she, without flinching, face the lightning of swords? Is she indifferent whether her life leaves her by the mouth or the throat? Is she settled, even, and content? This is what we have to look at, and from this you can judge of the vast differences between man and man. Is he:

"Sapiens, sibique imperiosus, Quern neque pauperies, neque mors, neque vincula terrent; Responsare cupidinibus, contemnere honores Fortis; et in seipso totus teres atque rotundus, Externi ne quid valeat per laeve morari; In quem manca ruit semper fortuna?"

["The wise man, self-governed, whom neither poverty, nor death, nor chains terrify: who has the strength to resist his appetites and despise honours: who is wholly self-contained, smooth and rounded, on whom no external thing can find purchase: whom fortune assails in vain." — Horace, Sat., ii. 7.]
Such a man is five hundred cubits above kingdoms and duchies; he is an absolute monarch in and over himself:
"Sapiens, . . . Pol! ipse fingit fortunam sibi;"
["By heaven, the wise man is the maker of his own fortune." — Plautus, Trin., ii. 2, 84.]
What is left for him to covet or desire?
"Nonne videmus, Nil aliud sibi naturam latrare, nisi ut, quoi Corpore sejunctus dolor absit, mente fruatur, Jucundo sensu, cura semotu' metuque?"
["Don't we see that nature asks nothing more for itself than that, free from bodily pain, it should enjoy its mind agreeably, exempt from care and fear." — Lucretius, ii. 16.]

Compare to such a man the common rabble of mankind, stupid and mean-spirited, servile, unstable, perpetually tossed about by the storm of various passions that drives them to and fro, and entirely dependent on others, and you will find a greater distance between them than between heaven and earth. And yet the blindness of common usage is such that we make little or no account of it; whereas if we consider a peasant and a king, a nobleman and a vassal, a magistrate and a private citizen, a rich man and a poor, the disparity appears vast, even though they differ no more, you might say, than in their breeches.

In Thrace the king was set apart from his people in a rather pleasant and peculiar manner: he had a religion to himself, a god all his own — whom his subjects were not allowed to worship — which was Mercury, while he himself disdained to have anything to do with theirs, Mars, Bacchus, and Diana. And yet these are merely pictures that make no essential difference. For just as you see actors in a play playing the part of a duke or an emperor on stage, and immediately afterward go back to their true original condition of valets and porters, so the emperor, whose pomp and lustre so dazzle you in public:
"Scilicet grandes viridi cum luce smaragdi Auto includuntur, teriturque thalassina vestis Assidue, et Veneris sudorem exercita potat;"
["Because he wears great emeralds richly set in gold, darting green light; and his sea-blue silken robe, worn from constant use, drinks up the sweat of Venus." — Lucretius, iv. 1123.]
— just peep behind the curtain, and you'll see nothing more than an ordinary man, and perhaps more contemptible than the meanest of his subjects:
"Ille beatus introrsum est, istius bracteata felicitas est;"
["The one is happy inwardly; the other's happiness is mere gilding." — Seneca, Ep., 115.]
Cowardice, irresolution, ambition, spite, and envy agitate him as much as anyone else:
"Non enim gazae, neque consularis Submovet lictor miseros tumultus Mentis, et curas laqueata circum Tecta volantes."
["For not treasures, nor the consular lictor, can drive away the miserable tumults of the mind, nor cares that fly around panelled ceilings." — Horace, Od., ii. 16, 9.]
Care and fear get at him even in the middle of his battalions:
"Re veraque metus hominum curaeque sequaces Nec metuunt sonitus armorum, nee fera tela; Audacterque inter reges, rerumque potentes Versantur, neque fulgorem reverentur ab auro."

["And in truth the fears and haunting cares of men do not fear the clash of arms or the points of spears, and move boldly among great kings and men in authority, with no respect for the glitter of gold." — Lucretius, ii. 47.]

Do fevers, gout, and apoplexies spare him any more than they do one of us? When old age weighs heavy on his shoulders, can the yeomen of his guard relieve him of the burden? When he is shaken by the apprehension of death, can the gentlemen of his bedchamber comfort and reassure him? When jealousy or some other caprice swims in his brain, can our compliments and ceremonies put him back in a good humour? The canopy embroidered with pearl and gold he lies under has no virtue against a violent fit of colic:
"Nec calidae citius decedunt corpore febres Textilibus si in picturis, ostroque rubenti Jactaris, quam si plebeia in veste cubandum est."
["Nor do burning fevers leave you any sooner if you toss on a couch of rich tapestry and in a robe of purple dye, than if you have to lie under a coarse blanket." — Lucretius, ii. 34.]

The flatterers of Alexander the Great convinced him he was the son of Jupiter; but one day he was wounded, and watching the blood stream from his cut, said: "Well, gentlemen, what say you now? Isn't this blood of a crimson colour, and purely human? It isn't the kind that Homer makes flow from the wounded gods." The poet Hermodorus had written a poem in honour of Antigonus, calling him the son of the sun. "The man who empties my chamber-pot," said Antigonus, "knows otherwise." He is, at best, only a man, and if he is deformed or ill-natured from birth, ruling the universe can't put him right:
"Puellae Hunc rapiant; quidquid calcaverit hic, rosa fiat,"
["Let girls carry him off; wherever he steps, let a rose spring up!" — Persius, Sat., ii. 38.]
What of all that, if he is a fool? Even pleasure and good fortune cannot be enjoyed without vigour and understanding:
"Haec perinde sunt, ut ilius animus; qui ea possidet Qui uti scit, ei bona; illi, qui non utitur recte, mala."
["Things are as is the mind of their possessor; to him who knows how to use them, they are goods; to him who misuses them, ills." — Terence, Heaut., i. 3, 21.]
Whatever the benefits of fortune are, they still require a palate to taste them. It's enjoyment, not possession, that makes us happy:

["It is not lands, or a heap of brass and gold, that has removed fevers from the body of the ailing owner, or cares from his mind. The possessor must be healthy if he hopes to make good use of his accumulated wealth. To the covetous or timorous man, his house and estate are as a picture to a blind man, or a fomentation to a sufferer from gout." — Horace, Ep., i. 2, 47.]

He is a sot, his taste is jaded and flat; he enjoys what he has no more than a man with a cold can taste canary wine, or a horse appreciates his rich trappings. Plato is right when he tells us that health, beauty, vigour, riches — and all the other things called goods — are equally evil to the unjust man as they are good to the just, and the evils the reverse. Where the body and mind are out of order, what use are these external conveniences? — considering that the slightest pin-prick, or the slightest stir of passion in the soul, is enough to deprive a man of the pleasure of being sole monarch of the world. At the first twinge of gout, what does it matter to be called Sir and Your Majesty?
"Totus et argento conflatus, totus et auro;"
["All made up of silver and gold." — Tibullus, i. 2, 70.]

Does he not forget his palaces and his grandeurs? If he is angry, does being a prince keep him from turning red and turning pale, and gnashing his teeth like a madman? Now, if he is a man of parts and of sound nature, royalty adds very little to his happiness:
"Si ventri bene, si lateri est, pedibusque tuis, nil Divitiae poterunt regales addere majus;"
["If it is well with your belly, your side, and your feet, regal riches can add nothing more." — Horace, Ep., i. 12, 5.]

He sees it's all counterfeit and trickery. He might even agree with King Seleucus, who said that the man who knew the weight of a sceptre would not stoop to pick it up if he saw it lying on the ground, so great and painful are the duties incumbent on a good king. To be sure, it can be no easy task to rule others, when we find it so hard to govern ourselves. And as to authority, that seems so charming, given the frailty of human judgment and the difficulty of choice in things new and doubtful, I am very much of the opinion that it is far easier and more pleasant to follow than to lead; and that it is a great satisfaction and ease of mind to have only one path to walk in, and to have no one to answer for but oneself:
"Ut satius multo jam sit parere quietum, Quam regere imperio res velle."
["It is much better to obey quietly than to wish to rule with command." — Lucretius, v. 1126.]

To which we may add Cyrus's saying that no man was fit to rule but one who was of greater worth than those he had to govern. But King Hiero in Xenophon goes further: in the very enjoyment of pleasure they are worse off than private men, because the ease and freedom they have to command anything they like takes the edge off the delight that ordinary folks find in it:
"Pinguis amor, nimiumque patens, in taedia nobis Vertitur, et, stomacho dulcis ut esca, nocet."
["Love in excess, and too readily available, turns to weariness for us, and, like sweetmeats to the stomach, does us harm." — Ovid, Amor., ii. 19, 25.]

Do we suppose the singing boys of the choir take any great delight in music? Satiety rather makes it tiresome and tedious for them. Feasts, balls, masquerades, and tournaments delight those who rarely see them and long to see them; but to those who go to such entertainments often, the taste grows flat and insipid. Nor do women so much delight those who make a common practice of the sport. The man who won't allow himself the leisure to be thirsty can never find the true pleasure of drinking. Farces and acrobatic tricks are pleasant for the audience, but wearisome work for those who perform them. And we see this when princes amuse themselves by sometimes disguising their rank for a while, stepping down to share the poor, ordinary way of living of the humblest of their people.
"Plerumque gratae divitibus vices Mundaeque parvo sub lare pauperum Coenae, sine aulaeis et ostro, Sollicitam explicuere frontem."
["The rich are often pleased with a change; and a plain supper under the small roof of the poor, without tapestries and purple, smooths the anxious brow." — Horace, Od., iii. 29, 13.]

Nothing is so distasteful and cloying as abundance. What appetite wouldn't be defeated by the sight of three hundred women at its mercy, as the Grand Signor has in his seraglio? And of his ancestors, what enjoyment or taste of sport did the one keep for himself, who never went hawking without seven thousand falconers? And beyond all this, I imagine that this lustre of greatness brings no small disturbance and uneasiness into the enjoyment of the most tempting pleasures: the great are too conspicuous and lie too open to everyone's view. Nor do I see why we should expect them more strictly to conceal their faults, since what is reckoned mere indiscretion in us, the people brand in them with the names of tyranny and contempt for the laws; and besides their proneness to vice, they are apt to feel that it adds to the pleasure to flout and trample on public conventions. Plato, in his Gorgias, defines a tyrant as one who in a city has licence to do whatever his own will leads him to do; and because of this impunity, the display and publicising of their vices often does more harm than the vice itself. Everyone fears being pried at and overlooked; but princes are watched even in their gestures, looks, and thoughts, the people believing they have a right to judge them. And besides, the blemishes of the great naturally appear larger because of the eminence and brilliance of the place they occupy, so that a mole or a wart on them shows up larger than a gaping cut would on others. This is why the poets pretend that the love-affairs of Jupiter were carried on in the disguise of so many borrowed shapes, and that among the many amorous adventures they lay at his charge there is only one, as I recall, in which he appears in his own majesty and grandeur.

But let us go back to Hiero, who further complains of the inconveniences he found in his royalty: he could not look around and travel the world freely, being a kind of prisoner within the bounds and limits of his own dominion; and in everything he did he was forever surrounded by a pressing crowd. And indeed, when I see our kings sitting alone at table, surrounded by so many people chattering around them and so many strangers staring at them, as they always are, I have often been moved more to pity than to envy their condition. King Alfonso used to say that in this respect asses were better off than kings, since their masters let them feed at their own ease and pleasure — a favour that kings cannot get from their servants. And it has never occurred to me that it could be of any great benefit to the life of a man of sense to have twenty people gabbling around him while he is on the privy; or that the services of a man worth ten thousand livres a year, or who has taken Casale or defended Siena, should be either more comfortable or more acceptable to him than those of a good groom of the chamber who knows his job. The advantages of sovereignty are in a manner only imaginary; every degree of fortune has in it some image of principality. Caesar calls all the lords of France, who hold their lands in free franchise, roitelets or petty kings; and in truth, the title of "sire" excepted, they go pretty far toward kingship. Just look in the provinces remote from court — Brittany, for example — and notice the train, the vassals, the officers, the employments, the service, the ceremony, and the state of a lord who lives retired from court in his own house, among his own tenants and servants; and observe besides the flight of his imagination: there is nothing more royal; he hears talk of his master once a year, as of a king of Persia, with no further acknowledgment of him than through some remote kinship his secretary keeps track of in some register. And, to tell the truth, our laws are easy enough — so easy that a French gentleman scarcely feels the weight of sovereignty pressing on his shoulders more than twice in his life. Real and effective subjection only touches those among us who voluntarily put their necks under the yoke, and who aim at wealth and honours through such services: for a man who loves his own fireside, and can manage his household without falling out with his neighbours or getting tangled up in lawsuits, is as free as the Doge of Venice.
"Paucos servitus, plures servitutem tenent."
["Few people are held by servitude; many hold themselves to it." — Seneca, Ep., 22.]

But what Hiero is most concerned about is that he finds himself stripped of all friendship, deprived of all mutual society, where the truest and most perfect enjoyment of human life lies. For what proof of affection and goodwill can I extract from someone who owes me, whether he likes it or not, everything he is able to do? Can I form any assurance of his real regard for me from his humble way of speaking and submissive manner, when these are ceremonies he isn't free to refuse? The honour we receive from those who fear us is not honour; those respects are due to royalty, not to me:
"Maximum hoc regni bonum est Quod facta domini cogitur populus sui Quam ferre, tam laudare."
["This is the greatest benefit of a kingdom: that the people is forced to praise the acts of its master as well as to bear them." — Seneca, Thyestes, ii. 1, 30.]

Don't I see that the wicked and the good king, the hated and the loved, are paid the same reverence? My predecessor was, and my successor will be, served with the same ceremony and state. If my subjects do me no harm, that's no evidence of any genuine affection — why should I take it as such, when it isn't in their power to do me harm if they would? No one follows me or obeys my orders out of any friendship between us; there can be no contracting of friendship where there is so little relation and exchange. My own height has put me out of any familiarity with or intelligence about men; there is too great a disparity and disproportion between us. They follow me either out of propriety and custom, or rather out of their attachment to my fortune than to me, hoping to increase their own. Everything they say to me or do for me is just outward paint and show, their freedom being constrained on all sides by the great power and authority I hold over them. I see nothing around me but what is dissembled and disguised.

When the Emperor Julian was one day applauded by his courtiers for his exact justice, he said: "I'd be proud of these praises, if they came from people who dared condemn or disapprove of the opposite, in case I should do it." All the real advantages of princes are shared by them with men of lesser condition (it's for the gods to mount winged horses and feed on ambrosia): their sleep is no different from ours, nor their appetite; the steel they arm themselves with is no better tempered than the steel we use; their crowns shield them no more from the rain or the sun.

Diocletian, who wore a crown so fortunate and so revered, resigned it to retire to the happiness of a private life; and some time later, when the necessity of public affairs required him to take up the burden again, he answered those who came to coax him: "You wouldn't try to persuade me to this if you'd seen the fine order of the trees I have planted in my orchard, and the fine melons I have sown in my garden."

In Anacharsis's opinion, the happiest state of government would be one where, all other things being equal, precedence was measured out according to a man's virtues, and exclusion according to his vices.

When King Pyrrhus was preparing for his expedition into Italy, his wise counsellor Cyneas, wanting to make him see the vanity of his ambition, said: "Well, sir, to what end are you making all this huge preparation?" "To make myself master of Italy," replied the king. "And what after that's done?" said Cyneas. "I'll cross over into Gaul and Spain," the king said. "And what then?" "Then I'll go and subdue Africa; and finally, when I have brought the whole world under my rule, I'll sit down and rest content at my own ease."

"For God's sake, sir," replied Cyneas, "tell me what stops you, if you like, from being in that condition right now? Why not at this very moment settle yourself in the state you say you're aiming at, and spare yourself all the labour and hazard in between?"
"Nimirum, quia non cognovit, quae esset habendi Finis, et omnino quoad crescat vera voluptas."
["Doubtless because he did not know what the limit of acquisition should be, and altogether how far real pleasure should grow." — Lucretius, v. 1431.]
I will close with an old verse that I think very apt to the point:
"Mores cuique sui fingunt fortunam."
["Each man's character shapes his own fortune." — Cornelius Nepos, Life of Atticus.]

title: Of sumptuary laws
paragraphs: The way our laws try to regulate idle and wasteful spending on food and clothing seems to me quite the opposite of what they intend. The right way would be to breed a contempt in men for silks and gold as vain, frivolous, and useless; whereas we, in fact, enhance their honour and price tag, which is hardly the way to put people off them. To pass a law that nobody but princes can eat turbot, or wear velvet and gold lace, and to forbid these things to ordinary people — what is that but to bring them into greater esteem, and set everyone all the more on edge to eat and wear them? Let kings leave off these emblems of grandeur; they have plenty of others. Such excesses are more excusable in anyone else than in a prince. We can learn from the example of several nations better ways to mark out social rank (which I do think is necessary in a state) without nourishing this kind of corruption and obvious nuisance. It is strange how quickly and easily custom in these indifferent things establishes itself and becomes authority. We had hardly been wearing plain cloth a year, in keeping with the court's mourning for Henry II, before silks had already fallen into such contempt with everyone that a man dressed in silk was automatically taken for a tradesman; silks were split between the doctors and surgeons, and although almost everyone else went about in the same kind of dress, there was nevertheless, in one thing or another, sufficient distinction of social rank. How suddenly do greasy chamois and linen doublets become the fashion in our armies, while all neatness and richness of dress fall into contempt? Let kings just take the lead and begin to give up this expense, and within a month the thing will be done throughout the kingdom, without edict or ordinance; we shall all follow. It ought rather to be proclaimed, on the contrary, that nobody should wear scarlet or goldsmith's work but courtesans and acrobats.

Zeleucus by the same kind of stratagem reclaimed the corrupted manners of the Locrians. His laws were that no freewoman should be allowed any more than one maid in attendance, unless she was drunk; nor was to go out of the city by night, wear gold jewellery, or go in an embroidered robe, unless she was a professed and public prostitute; that, apart from bravos, no man was to wear a gold ring, nor be seen in one of those effeminate robes woven in the city of Miletus. By these humiliating exceptions he cleverly diverted his citizens from superfluities and pernicious pleasures, and it was a project of great utility — attracting them to their duty and obedience through honour and ambition.
Our kings can do whatever they please in such external reformations; their own inclination, in this case, stands for law:
"Quicquid principes faciunt, praecipere videntur."
["Whatever princes themselves do, they seem to be prescribing." — Quintilian, Declam., 3.]

Whatever is done at court passes for a rule throughout the rest of France. Let the courtiers turn on those abominable breeches that show off so much of what should be concealed; these huge-bellied doublets that make us look like I-don't-know-what and are so unfit for wearing under arms; these long, effeminate locks of hair; this foolish custom of kissing what we hand to our equals, and our hands when we greet them, a ceremony in former times reserved only for princes. Let them not permit a gentleman to appear in any place of respect without his sword, with his clothes unbuttoned and uncinched, as if he had just come from the privy; and that, contrary to the custom of our forefathers and the particular privilege of the nobles of this kingdom, we stand a long time bareheaded before them in whatever place, and the same to a hundred others — so many tiercels and quartelets of kings we have these days, and other vicious innovations: the courtiers will see them all vanish at once and fall out of favour. These are, it's true, only superficial errors; but they are of bad omen, and enough to inform us that the whole structure is cracked and tottering when we see the rough-cast on our walls split and crumble.

Plato in his Laws considers nothing more pestilent in the consequences for his city than to give young men licence to introduce any change in their clothes, gestures, dances, songs, and exercises, from one form to another — shifting from this to that, chasing after novelties, and applauding the inventors; through which manners are corrupted and the old institutions come to be despised and held in contempt. In everything except what is evil, change is to be feared; even the change of seasons, winds, foods, and humours. And no laws are in their true credit but such as God has given so long a continuance to that no one knows their beginning, or that there ever was any other.

title: Of sleep
paragraphs: Reason directs that we should always go the same way, but not always at the same pace. And though a wise man ought not to give such free rein to human passions as to let them deviate from the right path, he may, without prejudice to his duty, leave it to them to hurry or to slow his speed, and not fix himself like a motionless and unfeeling Colossus. If virtue itself could put on flesh and blood, I believe the pulse would beat faster going on to an assault than going on to dinner: that is, there is a necessity that she should warm up and be stirred on this occasion. I have noticed, as something extraordinary, certain great men who in the highest enterprises and most important affairs have kept themselves in such a settled and serene calm as not to disturb their sleep. Alexander the Great, on the day fixed for that furious battle between him and Darius, slept so deeply and so long in the morning that Parmenio was forced to come into his chamber and, standing by his bedside, call him by name several times — the hour to go and fight compelling him to do so. The Emperor Otho, having resolved to kill himself that night, after settling his domestic affairs, dividing his money among his servants, and putting a good edge on a sword he had chosen for the purpose, and now waiting only to be sure that all his friends had got safely away, fell into so sound a sleep that the gentlemen of his chamber heard him snore. The death of this emperor has in it circumstances paralleling that of the great Cato, and particularly this just-mentioned one: for Cato, ready to dispatch himself, holding his hand only in expectation of the return of a messenger he had sent to bring word whether the senators he had sent away had got clear of the port of Utica, fell into so sound a sleep that those in the next room heard him snore; and when the man he had sent to the port had woken him to tell him that stormy weather had prevented the senators from putting to sea, he sent off another messenger, and composing himself again in bed, settled to sleep, and slept until the return of the last messenger brought him certain news that they were gone. We may further compare him with Alexander in the great and dangerous storm that threatened him through the sedition of the tribune Metellus, who, attempting to publish a decree to call Pompey with his army into the city at the time of Catiline's conspiracy, was opposed only — and stoutly — by Cato, so that very sharp language and bitter threats passed between them in the senate on the matter. But it was the next day, in the forenoon, that the controversy was to be decided, where Metellus, besides the favour of the people and of Caesar — at that time of Pompey's faction — was to appear accompanied by a rabble of slaves and gladiators; and Cato fortified only with his own courage and constancy; so that his relatives, household, and many of his virtuous friends were in great fear for him, to the point that some passed the whole night without sleep, eating, or drinking, for the danger they saw him in; his wife and sisters did nothing but weep and torment themselves in his house. He, on the contrary, comforted everyone, and after supping in his usual way, went to bed and slept soundly till morning, when one of his fellow tribunes roused him to go to the encounter. The knowledge we have of the greatness of this man's courage from the rest of his life may surely warrant us in judging that his composure came from a soul so far raised above such accidents that he disdained to let them take any more hold on his imagination than any ordinary incident.

In the naval engagement that Augustus won against Sextus Pompeius in Sicily, just as the battle was about to begin, he was so fast asleep that his friends had to wake him to give the signal for the fight: this was what gave Mark Antony occasion afterwards to reproach him that he hadn't the courage so much as to look on the order of his own squadrons with open eyes, and hadn't dared to show himself to the soldiers until Agrippa had brought him news of the victory won. But as for young Marius, who did much worse (on the day of his last battle against Sulla, after he had drawn up his army and given the word and signal for battle, he lay down under the shade of a tree to rest himself, and fell so soundly asleep that the rout and flight of his men could barely wake him, having seen nothing of the fight), he is said to have been at that time so utterly worn out with labour and lack of sleep that nature could hold out no longer. Now, on what has been said, the physicians may decide whether sleep is so necessary that our lives depend on it; for we read that King Perseus of Macedon, being a prisoner at Rome, was killed by being kept from sleep; but Pliny gives examples of people who have lived long without it. Herodotus speaks of nations where the men sleep and wake by half-years; and those who write the life of the sage Epimenides assert that he slept fifty-seven years on end.
